But for now, I am concluding the discussion and closing the ticket. 

Thank you for your patience,

Kadi 🙏

As to the second part of the ticket (regarding the concept of excessive):

* Clause 5.12.2 prohibits “excessively cancelling Ride-Hailing Services after indicating a willingness to fulfil them”.
* It references Clause 10.3.1, which deals with Bolt’s right to suspend access in response to material or persistent non-compliance.
* Clause 10.3.1 allows Bolt to suspend or terminate access if a Service Provider causes “material disruption or persistent failure to comply” — but again, no numbers or timeframes are defined.

My view:

Because no hard numbers are set, “excessive” is likely interpreted based on:

* Pattern of behaviour (e.g. X% of accepted trips cancelled within a time period),
* Impact (e.g. high cancellation rate during peak hours),
* Comparative benchmarks (e.g. higher than average for the market or similar drivers).

This gives Bolt an internal discretion to flag or sanction drivers based on local operational thresholds. However, clear internal rules or guidance would help reduce disputes and maintain fairness.

Hey all,

From Insurance:

Yes, I was aware of this change, as it will impact us when buying insurance, which is a pain as we spend a lot on Motor Insurance for Bolt Drive. 😥 

So I have already been trying to renew or place all our policies early, since anything done before 01.01.2026 will not be subject to this new 10% Insurance Premium Tax (IPT) being introduced in Lithuania.

For those unfamiliar, this IPT is technically called the _saugumo įnašas_ (security contribution) and is a new tax on non-life insurance premiums. It is a common form of taxation across much of the EU (see attached table for comparison, 10% for motor is on the lower side; Denmark is 42.9% and France is 33% :woozy_face: )

It works much like VAT, whereby it is applied and paid at source, and the insurer is responsible for collecting and remitting it to the tax authority (VMI).

For buyers of insurance (whether that is us, individual drivers, or any consumer), there is no extra administrative step as far as I know; it will simply appear as part of the insurance cost.

This will apply to all non-life insurance policies, meaning all drivers will see this increase in their premiums from next year, regardless of how frequently they use their vehicles.

Regarding personal taxes and whether drivers can claim this back, in countries such as Germany, France, and the UK, IPT is not recoverable through annual business tax returns like VAT. I am not sure how this will work in Lithuania, but I do not think we should be giving tax advice, as if we get it wrong, we could be held accountable. So it is probably safer to direct drivers to the local tax office or a qualified accountant for guidance.

Hi [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a]

I believe there are two realistic approaches, both entail some risk:

# This is considered an operational update to help drivers operate on the Bolt platform. In this case, no consent is required. This is riskier as even per your own view these communications can be considered promotional in nature.
# This is considered a direct marketing update, promoting the services of a third party. In this case, I believe requirements for hard opt-in consent will apply. I would consider the approach of obtaining consent during the phone call, as suggested [here|https://www.linklaters.com/insights/data-protected/data-protected---romania], to be problematic. I am aware that in Poland, such practice was found unlawful under case law, but I am not aware of this in RO. We would have to carefully ensure that the “pitch” of the marketing offer does not start before consent is given.

Realistically, the difference between both approaches would not be that hard, as in point 1, the driver would still have the option to object, so the result for Bolt is the same if they do.

In terms of risks, considering that this is essentially a B2B context (albeit B2C standards should be considered for drivers as they are not necessarily representing a company), the real risk in my view is to ensure drivers can very easily object and will not be contacted again + Bolt satisfies its transparency obligations, as you rightfully outlined before.

My POV, only alternative to points 1 and 2 would require updating the product to include a consent toggle at the moment of registration and underlying engineering work to connect this with the LCM system, which I would not consider realistic and proportionate for this scope of the project.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
So really, it's between options 1 and 2, which are not very different practically.

To in-fleet the vehicles, we must install our IoT solution (Lematics) with Teltonika hardware. Since Lematics had no prior experience with the VW Polo, they conducted a technical compatibility test. After testing one of our units, they informed us that full functionality — especially locking/unlocking — requires an internal system adjustment on the VW Polo.

This adjustment can only be performed by the OEM. It cannot be carried out by the dealer nor by Lematics/Teltonika. This has also been confirmed by the dealership.

Despite contacting multiple VW representatives over the past two weeks, we have not received clear guidance on how VW intends to solve this. I have attached the most recent response from their side. The root cause appears to be that, since mid-last year, all VW models must comply with UNECE cybersecurity regulations. As a result, such changes can only be implemented via ODIS-E (developer mode), which is OEM-restricted.

The dealership also informed us — confidentially — that VW has escalated this issue internally to top management, as the vehicles were not prepared system-wise for carsharing usage. VW was fully aware that the fleet would be used for free-floating carsharing and that we must install an IoT device.

To date:

* 64 out of 175 Polos have already been transported to Berlin and are parked at pur partners parking lot
* 64 vehicles have been stickered/branded
* We are incurring daily parking costs
* As there is still no clear solution from VW, we agreed with the dealer to suspend all in-fleeting activities (transport, registration, preparation, etc.)

If the required system modification cannot be implemented, the Polos cannot be used for our operations, and we would need to consider returning them to VW.

----

# What would be the implications — operational, financial, contractual — of returning all 175 Polos?
# Who would bear the costs already incurred on our side (transport, parking, branding, preparation)?
# What legal risks or challenges should we anticipate if we initiate a return or contract cancellation?

This topic has a *significant impact on our operations and our future partnership with VW*, and we need legal clarity urgently.
Please prioritize this request accordingly.

The usual approach is to confirm in writing that the claimant may attend *as an observer only*, subject to site-safety rules and to the engineers leading the inspection.

Refusing attendance without a strong reason (for example, safety or privacy concerns) can appear unco-operative and may be criticised later if the issue is raised in court. Allowing attendance, with a clear protocol (no handling, no recording without agreement), is seen as best practice.

Can you confirm if you’re happy for this to go ahead on that basis? If so, I can draft a short response back to the claimant’s solicitors confirming that the claimant may attend, subject to clear rules (observer only, no handling, and engineers to lead the inspection). *Please can you also confirm the date and time works for us.*

If we need to process a payout for such a driver, they need to be unblocked for that time (which can be risky of course, depending on the reason for the block).

Hi team,

Thanks for raising this. We’ve reviewed the legal risks and our view is that directly reaching out to fleet couriers during or after offboarding can create reclassification exposure, especially under Malta’s S.L. 452.127.

However, we understand that Malta is not facing reclassification claims for now and therefore we feel comfortable to recommend the following approach:

*After the fleet is officially offboarded*, Bolt may send a *neutral follow-up message* to the affected couriers. We propose the following wording:
_"If you are interested in continuing to use the Bolt Platform either independently or through another Fleet, please click here to see your available options."_

The link would lead to a landing page listing:

* Consenting fleets open to onboarding new couriers (with links to their external forms or sites).
* A separate link to Bolt’s standard self-employed courier registration form.


We believe this solution is a bit more safe, since:

* It avoids giving preferential direction toward self-employment.
* It presents Bolt as a neutral platform, not a recruiter or organizer of labour.
* It gives couriers autonomy to choose their path, helping rebut the presumption of employment.

Let us know if you’re aligned with this approach or have questions.

Thank you!

Translation needs rework, text needs editing, automated review findings:

{quote}*Comparison of Estonian and English E-Vehicle T&Cs – Identified Issues*

*Translation Errors*

* *Section 4.1 (Basic Pass)* – The phrase _“pay-as-you-go basis”_ was translated as *“läbisõidu põhjal”*, which literally implies _“based on distance traveled.”_ This could mislead users about the pricing model. The English original means paying per ride/use generally, not strictly by distance . A more accurate translation would clarify that it’s a usage-based or per-ride fee rather than distance-based.
* *Section 5.6 (Promo Codes)* – _“Promotional coupons or codes (‘Promo Codes’)”_ is translated as *“sooduskuponge või -koode (edaspidi sooduspakkumised)”* . The term *“sooduspakkumised”* means _special offers_ in Estonian, which is broader than specific promo codes. This may reduce clarity – readers might not immediately connect _sooduspakkumised_ with discount codes. Using a term like _“sooduskoodid”_ (promo codes) or explicitly defining it as such would be more precise.
* *Section 8.2 (Acceptable Use)* – The final rule in English _“other action which is deemed as inappropriate for use of the App.”_ appears unnumbered after 8.2.14. In Estonian it is translated (*“tegutseda viisil, mida võib rakenduse kasutamisel ebasobivaks pidada”*) but also left without a clause number . While this mirrors the source, it results in an awkward hanging sentence. It’s a minor translation fidelity issue, but primarily a formatting error from the original (see Reference Errors below).



*Omissions*

* *Section 6.9.2 (Liability Limits)* – The English text excludes _“loss of profit_ *_or anticipated savings_*_.”_ The Estonian version only mentions *“saamata jäänud tulu”* (lost profit) and omits _anticipated savings_ . This omission narrows the scope of the liability exclusion. The translator should include a phrase for anticipated savings (e.g. _“või saamata jäänud kokkuhoid”_) to fully reflect the original clause.
* *Blank Clauses (English source)* – The English original contains a couple of numbered clauses with no content (e.g. *1.3.4* and *8.2.13*). The Estonian translation mirrors these gaps: section *1.3.4* is empty and *8.2.13* is skipped with no text . No substantive text is lost here – these appear to be intentional or formatting blanks in the source. Aside from the _“anticipated savings”_ phrase noted above, we did *not* find any full clauses present in English that were completely missing in the Estonian version; all main sections and annexes are translated.

 

*Grammatical and Typographic Errors (Estonian Text)*

* *Section 5.3 (Subscriptions)* – The sentence *“Te lubata meil võtta…*” is grammatically incorrect . *“Te lubata”* should be *“Te lubate”* (second person plural present tense) to read “You allow us to charge…”. This appears to be a conjugation typo.
* *Section 2.5 (Modified devices)* – Mid-sentence, the pronoun *“Me”* (We) is capitalized in *“…et Me ei vastuta kahjude eest…”* . In Estonian, *“me”* should be lowercase here. The capital *“Me”* is likely a typographical error, as elsewhere the text correctly uses lowercase _meie_/_me_ for Bolt.
* *Section 5.3 (Withdrawal period)* – _“14päevase taganemisperioodi”_ is missing a hyphen. It should be written *“14‑päevase”* (with a hyphen) to properly form the compound adjective .
* *Section 5.7.3* – The phrase _“_*_120 euro_* _suurune sõidutasu”_ is inconsistent in case. In Estonian usage it should be *“120 eurot suurune sõidutasu”* (partitive case for the amount) . For comparison, the text correctly uses _“500 eurot”_ in section 5.7.4 . This is a minor grammatical consistency issue.
* *Section 5.10 (In-App payments)* – The text reads *“Me võime kinda ajavahemiku eri tehingud kokku liita…”* . *“kinda”* is a typo and should be *“kindla”* (with an *l*, meaning “fixed period of time”). This typographical error could confuse the meaning of the sentence.

 

*Reference and Numbering Errors*

* *Section 5 (Payment clauses)* – There is a numbering mix-up in the Estonian text for clauses 5.8 and 5.9. The content corresponding to English *Section 5.8* (municipal fines and charges) is correctly labeled *5.8* in Estonian, but the sub-points under it are incorrectly numbered *5.7.1* and *5.7.2* instead of 5.8.1 and 5.8.2 . Furthermore, the paragraph corresponding to English *Section 5.9* was mis-labeled as a second *5.8* . This caused all subsequent sections to be off by one: e.g. English 5.9 appears as 5.8, 5.10 as 5.9, and so on through 5.14 (which is marked 5.13 in Estonian). This numbering error can confuse cross-references. For instance, there are two 5.8 headings in a row in the Estonian document. (By context, it’s clear what is meant, but the numbering should be corrected to align with the source.)
* *Annex A Label* – The Estonian document does not explicitly label *Annex A* as “Lisa A.” Instead, a stray heading *“TELLIMUSLENDUDE LEPINGU”* (unrelated text meaning “charter flights contract”) appears before the Annex A content . This is almost certainly an error. The actual Annex A content (the _“Elektriliste sõidukite üldised sõidueeskirjad”_ riding rules) follows immediately, but without a proper title line to mark it as *Lisa A* . This could mislead readers or disrupt the document’s structure. Annex B, by contrast, is correctly titled *“LISA B – Taganemisvormi näidis”* in the Estonian version . The Annex A heading should likewise be fixed.
* *Numbering Gap in Acceptable Use* – As noted, *clause 8.2.13* is missing content and is skipped in numbering in both versions . The next item “use of automated systems…” is labeled 8.2.14, and the final catch-all _inappropriate action_ item is not numbered (treated as a continuation of 8.2.14 with an “or”) . In the Estonian text, this final item appears as an unnumbered sentence after 8.2.14, which can be confusing. Essentially, the Acceptable Use list jumps from 8.2.12 to 8.2.14, leaving a perceived gap. This is a source text issue, but it affects the Estonian document’s coherence as well.
* *Cross-References* – Most cross-references were translated correctly (e.g. _“in accordance with Section 10.1”_ → *“kooskõlas punktis 10.1 sätestatuga”* , and references to Riding Rules Section 3, etc.). However, due to the numbering shifts mentioned, references to section numbers in *Section 5* could be misaligned. For example, _“…in section 3 of the Riding Rules…”_ was accurately rendered as *“sõidureeglite punktis 3”* . No incorrect cross-reference words (like wrong section numbers or annex letters) were found aside from the misnumbering issues themselves.

Do we care about persistence?* *Yes, absolutely.* This is *not* a cache usage pattern (like caching API responses). We are using Redis as a *Vector Database* and *State Store*.

* *Use Case:* It stores the *Long-Term Knowledge Base* (Vector Embeddings of our documentation) and *Active Chat History*.
* *Impact of Data Loss:* If Redis flushes, the AI instantly forgets all ongoing conversations and we have to re-scrape/re-index the entire Confluence documentation database.
* *Persistence config:* Standard AOF (Append Only File) persistence is sufficient for our volume (~150 messages/day), but it must be enabled. We need a {{noeviction}} policy to ensure memory stability.

Correction: “…bojāts vai remontējamā stāvoklī, no Jums tiks paņemta maksa…”. (Notably, the same term is used correctly as “remontējamā stāvoklī” in Section 5.7.2 of the Latvian text ￼, indicating this was a slip in 4.3.4.)

It seems to be aiming for “agreement to immediately inform Us,” but mixing a noun (piekrišanu) with a verb phrase. Correction: Use a finite verb clause. For example: “Jūs piekrītat nekavējoties informēt Mūs, ja esat pamanījis nesankcionētu piekļuvi Jūsu Kontam…”. This way, “piekrītat” governs the verb “informēt” directly, making the sentence grammatically clear.

Correction: “…kas uzskaitīti iepriekš 3.1.4. un 3.1.5. punktā.” (or “…punktos 3.1.4. un 3.1.5.”). This uses punkti (points/clauses) and in plural, which is the proper way to refer to multiple sub-sections in Latvian legal text.

h1. *Comparative Analysis of Lithuanian Translation vs English Source Text*

*Translation Errors (with Lithuanian rewording suggestions)*

* *Clause 1.1* – _“yra sudėtinė dalis sutarties (Sutartis)”_ is a misleading rendering of _“constitute the agreement (‘Agreement’)”_. The Lithuanian implies the Terms are only part of a contract, rather than the contract itself . *Suggestion:* _“Šios paslaugų sąlygos sudaro sutartį (toliau – Sutartis)…”_, conveying that the Terms *form* the Agreement.
* *Clause 1.1* – _“Mūsų padalinių”_ for _“our affiliates”_ is imprecise . _Padaliniai_ means internal divisions, not separate affiliated companies. *Suggestion:* _“mūsų susijusių įmonių”_ (or _“dukterinių bendrovių”_), which correctly refers to affiliated companies.
* *Clause 1.3.3* – The phrase _“bet kurie kiti Programėlėje rodomi dalykai – Skatinimo kodų sąlygos, …”_ is stylistically poor . Using _“dalykai”_ (“things”) in legal text is unclear. Also, _“Skatinimo kodų sąlygos”_ for _“Promo Code terms”_ is non-standard (literal “encouragement codes”) . *Suggestions:* Replace _“dalykai”_ with _“informacija”_ (or omit it), and use a more usual term for promo codes (e.g. _“Akcijos (promo) kodų sąlygos”_). For example: _“… ir kita Programėlėje pateikiama informacija, įskaitant akcijos kodų sąlygas, visas instrukcijas, vadovus (įskaitant…vadovus) ir kitus nurodymus.”_
* *Clause 1.4* – _“Mes pasiliekame teisę bet kuriuo metu papildyti šias Sąlygas…”_ only denotes adding to the Terms , whereas the English _“make changes to this Agreement”_ includes any amendments . *Suggestion:* _“…teisę bet kuriuo metu pakeisti ar papildyti šias Sąlygas…”_, ensuring it covers modifications, not just additions.
* *Clause 3.1.2* – _“Pasirinktasis mokėjimų metodas”_ (lit. “Chosen payments method”) is grammatically off . The intended term is singular. *Suggestion:* _“Pasirinktasis mokėjimo metodas”_, aligning with the defined _“Elected Payment Method”_. (E.g.: _“…pvz. ‘Bolt Business’ arba ‘Family Account’ (toliau – Pasirinktasis mokėjimo metodas)”_.)
* *Clause 4.3.2* – Inconsistent terminology for the *Riding Rules*. The text uses _“Važiavimo taisykles”_ here , but _“Vairavimo taisykles”_ was defined in Annex A . This could confuse the reader. *Suggestion:* use the same term as in the definition, e.g. _“Vairavimo taisykles”_, throughout.
* *Clause 4.3.4* – The translation erroneously refers to _“automobilis”_ (“automobile”) when describing returning the e-vehicle, and defines _“Leistinos automobilio statymo vietos”_ (“permitted car parking places”) . This is a carryover from car-sharing terms and is incorrect for scooters/bikes. *Suggestion:* refer to the _“el. transporto priemonė”_ instead of “automobilis”. For example: _“…grąžinsite el. transporto priemonę į Leistiną parkavimo vietą tokios pačios būklės, kokios ji buvo nuomos pradžioje…”_. Likewise, _“Leistinos parkavimo vietos”_ is preferable as a defined term instead of _“Leistinos automobilio statymo vietos”_.
* *Clause 4.3.4* – The cross-reference to _“5.4.2 punkte”_ is incorrect . In the English source, the charge for damage refers to *Section 5.6.2* . This misnumbering could misdirect the reader. *Suggestion:* change to _“kaip numatyta 5.6.2 punkte”_ for accuracy.
* *Clause 4.6.2* – The phrase _“…atitiktų 3.1.4 ir 3.1.5 punktuose išvardytas reikalavimus atitinkančias sąlygas.”_ is convoluted . It attempts to say “meet the requirements listed in 3.1.4 and 3.1.5” but mixes plural/singular. *Suggestion:* _“…atitiktų 3.1.4 ir 3.1.5 punktuose išvardytus reikalavimus.”_ This clearer phrasing omits the unnecessary _“sąlygas”_.
* *Clause 4.6* (Group Rides) – _“Priimantysis subjektas”_ for *“Host”* is overly formal and abstract . Since it refers to the person initiating a group ride, a simpler term would improve clarity. *Suggestion:* use _“Priimantysis”_ alone (or even _“Grupinės kelionės iniciatorius”_ if acceptable), and ensure consistent use of this term. For instance: _“…galime leisti Jums (Priimančiajam) atrakinti kelias….”_. This would read more naturally while still defining “Host”.
* *Section 5 Title* – _“Mokėjimai ir sumos”_ is an unusual translation of “Payment and Fees” . _Sumos_ (“sums”) is vague in context. *Suggestion:* _“Mokėjimai ir mokesčiai”_ or _“Mokėjimo sąlygos ir įkainiai”_, which more precisely cover payments and fees.
* *Clause 5.7.5* – Again the word _“automobilis”_ appears, e.g. _“Automobilio stovėjimo kontrolės mokestis”_ and _“netinkamai pastatytas automobilis”_ . Using “automobile” is inappropriate for e-vehicles (scooters/bikes). *Suggestion:* _“Stovėjimo kontrolės mokestis”_ (omit “automobilio”) and _“netinkamai pastatyta transporto priemonė”_. For example: _“…Mes galime iš Jūsų imti 6 EUR mokestį (Stovėjimo kontrolės mokestis)…”_ and _“…netinkamai pastatyta el. transporto priemonė… yra šios Sutarties pažeidimas…”_.
* *Clause 6.1.3* – Inconsistent term for *Riding Rules* yet again: _“laikysitės Važiavimo taisyklių”_ . This should match the defined _“Vairavimo taisyklės”_. The fluctuation between _Važiavimo_ and _Vairavimo_ is a translation inconsistency. *Suggestion:* use _“Vairavimo taisyklių”_ here for consistency with Annex A .
* *Clause 8.3* – The text references _“kelionių taisyklių ar saugos priemonių rinkinio”_ , presumably meaning the *Riding Rules or Safety Toolkit*, but neither term matches earlier definitions (_“Vairavimo taisyklės”_, _“Saugos komplektas”_). *Suggestion:* use the defined terms. For example: _“…Tinkamo naudojimo taisyklių, Vairavimo taisyklių ar Saugos komplekto nurodymų nesilaikymas…”_. This ensures the reader recognizes the same rules defined in Annex A and clause 1.3.2 .
* *Clause 8.3* – _“Priimtino naudojimosi taisyklių”_ is used as a synonym for _“Tinkamo naudojimo taisyklės”_, the established term for *Rules of Acceptable Use* . Mixing terms can be confusing. *Suggestion:* stick to one term. Since _“Tinkamo naudojimo taisyklės”_ was introduced in clause 8.1, use that throughout (e.g. _“Tinkamo naudojimo taisyklių… nesilaikymas yra esminis pažeidimas…”_).
* *Clause 10.2* – The assignment clause is translated in an unclear way. The English allows Bolt to assign the agreement or any supplemental agreements at its discretion. The Lithuanian _“visi papildomi susitarimai būtų automatiškai priskirti Mums ir patikėti Mūsų nuožiūrai”_ is hard to parse. *Suggestion:* clarify the sentence. For example: _“Jūs sutinkate, kad Mes galime savo nuožiūra perleisti šią Sutartį ir bet kokius papildomus susitarimus kitam subjektui.”_ This makes it clear Bolt can assign the agreement.
* *Annex A, clause 1.1* – The phrase _“kurį apima be apriboji šie dalykai:”_ contains a typo and grammar error . It attempts to translate _“that includes, without limitation, the following:”_. *Suggestion:* _“kurį, be apribojimų, sudaro šie elementai:”_. Notably, _“be apriboji”_ should be _“be apribojimų”_ (the plural form) .
* *Annex B (Model withdrawal form)* – The Lithuanian text reads _“Pranešu, kad atsisakau savo sutikimo teikti šią paslaugą: Išankstinio mokėjimo naudojimas įsigyjant Paslaugas.”_ . This is a mistranslation of “I withdraw from my contract for the provision of the following service: purchase of Package Pass…”. The current wording implies the *consumer withdraws their consent to provide the service*, which is incorrect (the consumer is the recipient, not provider). *Suggestion:* Reword in line with EU model forms, e.g.: _“Pranešu, kad atsisakau sutarties dėl šios paslaugos teikimo: Išankstinio mokėjimo paslaugos (Paslaugų paketo) įsigijimo.”_. This phrasing makes it clear the consumer is withdrawing from the contract for that service.

* *Missing Clause 1.3.4:* In both the English and Lithuanian texts, section 1.3 skips from 1.3.3 to 1.3.5 with no content for 1.3.4 . h2. *Grammatical and Typographic Errors*

* *Typographical error in Annex A 1.1:* _“be apriboji šie dalykai”_ is a typo – _“apriboji”_ is missing the plural ending . It should read _“be apribojimų šie dalykai”_ ( “without limitation, the following items”). This is a clear typographical error in the Lithuanian text.
* *Case Agreement and Grammar (Annex A 1.1):* _“kurį apima … šie dalykai”_ is grammatically misaligned (object _kurį_ vs. plural subject _šie dalykai_). A grammatically correct construction would be _“kurį sudaro … šie punktai”_. This error likely resulted from a direct translation without adjusting for Lithuanian sentence structure.
* *“įsipareigojimus atitinkančias sąlygas” (Clause 4.6.2):* The phrase _“reikalavimus atitinkančias sąlygas”_ is redundant and ungrammatical . The word _“sąlygas”_ (conditions) is unnecessary when _“atitikti reikalavimus”_ (meet the requirements) suffices. The sentence can be simplified to eliminate this mistake (as suggested above).
* *Inconsistent Use of Defined Terms (capitalization):* The translation inconsistently capitalizes defined terms and uses varied terminology:
** _Paslaugos zona_ vs. _Paslaugų zona:_ In some places “Service Area” is _“Paslaugos zona”_ (capitalized, singular) , elsewhere _“Paslaugų zona”_ (genitive plural) or _“Paslaugų teikimo zonos”_ . This inconsistency is grammatical – it should be uniform (e.g., always _Paslaugos zona_ as defined in 1.3.5).
** _Paskyra:_ The term for Account was defined with capital P (_“Paskyra”_ in 2.2) . The translation sometimes uses lowercase _“paskyra”_ (e.g., _“Jūsų paskyra”_【31†L260-L264}) and sometimes uppercase (e.g., _“savo Paskyrą”_【31†L311-L314}). For a defined term, the usage should be consistent (preferably capitalized) to avoid confusion.
** Pronouns: The translation capitalizes _Jūs_ (You) consistently as is customary in formal Lithuanian, but also capitalizes _Mes/Mūsų_ (We/Our) in mid-sentence (e.g., _“…Mes neprisiimame atsakomybės…”_【39†L73-L77}). Capitalizing “we” is not standard Lithuanian and appears to imitate the English style. It’s a stylistic inconsistency but does not change meaning; the final text should decide on a convention (usually, pronouns referring to the company are lowercase in Lithuanian).
** _Vairavimo taisyklės_ vs. _Važiavimo/kelionių taisyklės:_ The Riding Rules are inconsistently named (see Translation Errors above). This is also a consistency issue; the term _“Vairavimo taisyklės”_ (as defined in Annex A) should be used throughout to maintain grammatical consistency and clarity.
** _Saugos komplektas:_ Similarly, the Safety Toolkit is defined as _“Programėlės saugos komplektas”_ . In clause 8.3, it’s called _“saugos priemonių rinkinys”_ . This variance can confuse readers and is a terminological inconsistency. It should be uniform (preferably _Saugos komplektas_ as defined).
* 
* *Punctuation and structure:* Several sentences in the translation are overly long or use informal connectors:
** In clause 5.7.3, _“taip pat būsite apmokestinti … priklausomai nuo laiko, kurio prireiks…”_ is a run-on sentence in Lithuanian. Consider breaking into separate sentences or using semicolons for clarity.

However, the last item in 8.2 (the catch-all “other actions” clause) was not properly numbered or punctuated (see Reference Errors). This creates a grammatical fragment at the end of the list. It should either end in a period or be integrated into the previous item with a semicolon.
* 
* *Minor Style and Orthography:*
** *Currency format:* The text uses _“100 eurų”_, _“30 EUR”_, etc. For consistency, it’s better to pick one format. In Lithuanian, the normative format would be _“100 Eur”_ or _“100 €”_ (with capital E only in the ISO code when isolated). While not legally critical, using a uniform style (e.g., _EUR_ in all caps or _Eur_ with capital E only) would be typographically consistent.

Just ensure letters like _“h)”_ are followed by a clear clause – e.g., in 1.1(h) the sentence _“laikytis instrukcijų… kurios pateikiamos… užsakymo metu.”_ is a bit disconnected due to line breaks. This may be a formatting issue in the document rather than a translation error, but the final layout should keep the sub-point with its text for readability.
** *Spelling:* Aside from _“apriboji”_ (typo) noted above, the translation spelling is generally correct. We did not find misspelled words beyond that typographical slip.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Key concerns
{panel}

* We collected documents like IDs or residence permits strictly for compliance purposes (for transport service provision). Using them to infer or filter language ability would be an unapproved secondary use and not transparent to the driver.
* Automatically enrolling only some drivers, while forcing others into an interview, risks perceived unequal treatment. This could lead to formal complaints or reputational damage. While this is not a directly privacy concern, but this might raise privacy complaints: drivers who feel discriminated will take this as an opportunity/angle to come at us from.
* If we don’t already collect language info, where are we pulling it from? Making assumptions based on nationality or name is problematic. 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Privacy-aligned path forward
{panel}

If we want to proceed in a transparent and fair way:

* Make the category opt-in (voluntary/self declaration) - all drivers (local or foreign) can express interest via a clear campaign or form
* Avoid guessing based on documents - don’t use driver-uploaded documents for language classification
* Use a neutral, external assessor - if we need interviews to check language proficiency, I suggest considering partnering with a local language school or agency to do assessments professionally
* Keep drivers informed - be clear about what this category is, how it works, and how language skill is determined

I imagine it will be more efficient to provide our Legal and Privacy advice together to save on overlapping advice / confusing the stakeholders. I have done a centralised assessment on HVC here ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14CmJpL-aSKQ82zKFbWsw_Xszjh9uzeEkOMkxvRd3gzI/edit?tab=t.0]) - the key points for the UK are as follows (i) 

* *In-app guidance / driver transparency materials* ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.c383kapuni8h]) need to contain more details, as currently they are too high level and are likely to prompt questions and complaints from drivers. This is particularly sensitive in the UK, given concerns about transparency around how trip allocation works (see the ICO inquiry from earlier this year). My preference would be to include the following:
** An explanation of which categories as considered ‘premium’, and why Bolt needs to measure KPIs to determine eligibility for these categories;
** An overview of which KPIs will be used to determine eligibility;
** Emphasis that: (i) drivers will be sent warnings before being excluded; and (ii) exclusion is not permanent if KPIs are met; and
** A hyperlink to Bolt driver privacy notice.
* *Warning comms* should be sent (in good time) in advance of category exclusion (again, this is particularly important in the UK after the ICO investigation). Currently, the template for such comms ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.4ntyngmbuskj]) is not transparent enough regarding why a driver is being excluded and what they can do about it. My preference would be to include the following:
** Clear indications of specific KPIs which have not been met (e.g., the comms currently mention rating / score / acceptance rate, but not finished orders / completion rate); and
** Details on which threshold has not been made (if feasible).
** *Exclusion comms* should contain the same level of detail, as well as information on how long the driver has to appeal / what they can do to regain access.
* As already advised by Central Legal, we should have a *clearly structured appeal process* (which is subject to human review, in light of the ICO inquiry), that is clearly documented internally.
* Unless strictly necessary, *we should not use acceptance rate as a KPI* in the UK, being a high-risk market.
* For any *photos submitted as part of quality inspections*, these should be securely stored and in a way where it is easy to locate and extract them if needed (e.g,, for DSARs).

Happy to discuss the above this week so that we can go back to the business as a united front 🙂

Then just change of the title of depreciation profile is not possible, unless,

* all depreciation posted is canceled: but to do it , you will need to open all previous periods, when depreciation was recorded, plus if there were disposals during the year within the same spend category at this entity, then you will need to first reinstate such assets, otherwise the system won’t allow to cancel depreciation.  And then of course, to dispose again the assets

OR you can dispose the asset and register it again with correct depreciation profile, adjusted historical accumulated depreciation, remaining life … and create manual journal to reverse disposal in accounting. Which again creates “unnecessary” journals and manual work.

_Dear Carmen,_

_Thank you for your continued collaboration as we work toward finalizing the agreement. We appreciate the updates shared in the latest draft and have reviewed them closely, and happily say that we are getting closer to a final version._

_In this new version, that you can find_ [_here_|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Z6th0ETLamhDLXrHDodKg_KlDyFuUTax/edit]_, you will see that:_

* _we accepted a lot of your changes or refusal of our proposed changes;_
* _we made v/ small amendments where needed, in order to make sure everything is clear; and_
* _we did not accept all changes proposed in clauses 5 e), f) and g) and clause 8._

_Regarding the last point, these are three key areas where we believe further alignment is necessary to reflect what was initially agreed and to ensure fairness and operational clarity._

# *_Clause 5(e) – Total Loop Length of Digital Advertising Space_*

_We respectfully request that the clause reflect the originally position, which is that our Share of Voice (SOV) should remain fixed, and any material increase in the total loop length — regardless of the cause — should trigger a proportional adjustment to the Monthly Fee._

_As currently worded, the clause allows for loop increases without automatic adjustment unless they are “material” and caused by the Concessionaire. This introduces ambiguity and could allow for reductions in exposure without fee relief. Exposure consistency is a fundamental basis of this agreement._

_We would appreciate reinstating our version to preserve that principle._

# *_Clauses 5(f) & (g) – Placement Changes and Related Costs_*

_This section is of critical importance to us, as it directly impacts the predictability of our advertising investment. We respectfully request the following points be restored or clarified:_

* _The Monthly Fee should remain unchanged even if a substitute placement carries a higher nominal rate._
* _The Advertiser should have the right to select from proposed alternative placements, rather than being passively assigned a location._
* _A clear pro-rata credit mechanism should apply if no satisfactory substitute is available._
* _Any exceptions regarding reprinting/reinstallation costs — particularly those arising from internal “operational reasons” — should be narrowly defined or removed to avoid unforeseen financial exposure._

# *_Remedies_*

_It might seem that we shifted the all clause, but that is not the case._
_We accepted most of your redaction, but made an adjustment having in consideration clause 5 (e), (f) and (g), which, as explained above, are critical to us._

_We also believe it is essential for the termination framework to be balanced and clearly defined. In particular:_

* _The termination rights and remedies should be mutual, allowing both parties to exit the agreement in cases of material breach._
* _The 10-day cure period should apply clearly and consistently._
* _Clauses on liquidated damages and deposit retention should include reasonable boundaries to ensure predictability and fairness._

_We believe these changes would improve clarity, reduce legal uncertainty, and ensure the contract reflects a fair and workable commercial relationship for both sides._

_Bolt has always been extremely flexible and collaborative in its commercial dealings with your team, and we deeply value our relationship. However, in this particular case, the scale of Bolt’s investment is significant, and the agreement spans a long period. For that reason, we would truly appreciate some flexibility from your side as well — we need to ensure that we are not entering into a contract that could result in unanticipated exposure or financial imbalance._

_We look forward to your feedback._

_Warm regards,_

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

The issue escalated in [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/690846102|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/690846102] is a real issue. 

Before the customer placed an order 21 Nov 2025, 21:38:32 (UTC+01:00) they already had a negative balance of 20.34 PLN as Bolt was not able to capture the full amount. 

The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 29.84 PLN, but order price was just 9.5 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 20.34 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 9.5 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 29.84 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 9.5 PLN. 

29.84 PLN - 9.5 PLN = 20.34 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB.

No special formalities are required. However, we recommend sending a written demand for payment specifying the amount and the period for which statutory commercial delay interest is calculated.

Hi [~accountid:61374989bba6c7006a2616ba],

Following our internal review of the Cyprus Fleet Agreements, here’s the legal view:

Implementing *courier-level blocking for low acceptance rate* does create some *reclassification risk*, but Cyprus is not currently among the highest-risk jurisdictions, especially if this applies *only to fleet couriers*. In that sense, it is mainly a *business decision*.

However, the current CY Fleet Agreements do *not* include any clauses allowing courier-level performance measures or blocking — they only set fleet-level obligations, and there are no unilateral amendment rights.

If the team wants to proceed, our preferred approach is to move fleets to a new *Fleet Agreement*, where we can include clear performance standards and a clause enabling unilateral changes with 15 days’ notice.

If this is urgent and you cannot wait for new agreements, there is an *interim workaround*: we can rely on the *General T&Cs*, which allow Bolt to restrict access where a fleet’s activity interferes with platform operations or shows no genuine intention to provide services (clauses 4.3.2 and 4.3.3). This gives us a defensible basis to temporarily block underperforming couriers as a limitation on the fleet’s access, not as direct control over workers.

If we go ahead, both the *courier* and the *fleet* should be notified of any suspension, emphasising that the restriction applies to the fleet account.

Let me know which route you prefer and we’ll support accordingly.

Many thanks!

Risks of Option 2: Privacy team considers that automatic enrolment will likely cause discomfort or raise reputational concerns with drivers. If they complain to the local regulator, there is high chance that Bolt will be investigated and this practice would be found unlawful.

* If you choose this route, consent could be collected in several ways - for example, an in-app banner or notification, or an email with a consent form. Using the app would be the most effective and consistent method.

Collecting consent will require some operational effort and coordination with Product and LCM. We are not aware of any existing functionality that could be reused for this purpose.

h2. 1. Translation of the request

The police (OOPZ Nitra – východ) refer to:

* § 60(1)(e) of Act No. 372/1990 Coll. on Offences
Authorities competent to clarify offences may, when clarifying an offence, require submission of necessary documents, especially files and other written materials, from relevant bodies. Natural and legal persons are obliged to promptly comply.

Facts described:
An alleged petty theft offence under § 50(1)(c) of the Offences Act: the passenger allegedly did not pay for a ride from Cabaj–Čápor to Žirany on 11 August 2025. The police request contact details of the person who ordered that specific ride, to summon them to give an explanation.

----

h2. 2. Overview: what is requested, by whom, purpose, legal basis

Data requested:
Contact details of the rider for one specific trip (identity + contact info).

Authority:
Police – Obvodné oddelenie PZ Nitra – východ (Slovak Police).

Purpose:
To identify and hear the rider in an administrative offence investigation for non-payment.

Legal basis cited:
§ 60(1)(e) of Act No. 372/1990 Coll. on Offences.

----

h2. 3. Legal basis assessment

h3. a. Is this basis listed as accepted by Bolt?

Under Slovakia in the Accepted Legal Bases list:
Code of Criminal Procedure (Trestný poriadok) and Act on the Police Force (171/1993) are listed.
The Offences Act 372/1990 is not listed as an accepted basis.

In the Not Accepted list for Slovakia, we have:
❌ Article 56(1) of the Slovak Offences Act.

This means Bolt has explicitly rejected Section 56(1), not the entire Act. The police rely on Section 60(1)(e). That provision is not flagged as rejected.

h3. b. Is § 60(1)(e) a valid legal obligation under Slovak law?

Yes.
§ 60(1)(e) grants police the power, during an offence investigation, to demand necessary documents and information, and imposes a mandatory cooperation obligation on legal entities. This is materially similar to other cooperation duties Bolt accepts under criminal procedure laws in other markets.

It is a specific legal duty imposed directly by statute.
There is no indication that this provision applies only to employers or would otherwise exclude Bolt.

Therefore the legal basis is valid for disclosure.

----

h2. 4. Scope and proportionality

The request is narrow:

* One ride.
* One date.
* Clear context (non-payment).
* Only contact details of the person who ordered the trip.

This is proportionate and directly linked to the stated purpose. No excessive data requested.
We should limit disclosure strictly to what is needed: typically name, phone number, email and any identifier visible in the order.

No ride history or unrelated metadata.

----

h2. 5. Decision and instructions

h3. Approval

The requested disclosure can be made.

Hi [~accountid:712020:f02d2cce-cc32-4a0f-bc47-cc4305d9c4b8], I have discussed your questions with the privacy team who have kindly set out the answers below. Please let me know if you have any questions.

# *Disclosure of the driver’s licensing authority*

We should _not_ share the driver’s licensing authority with the rider. While it may seem like administrative information, in context it forms part of the driver’s regulatory record and is therefore considered _personal data_. Disclosing it would involve sharing the driver’s personal information, which we are not permitted to do.

Importantly, withholding this information does _not_ prevent the rider from raising a complaint. They can report the issue to Bolt, the police, or the licensing authority for the area where the trip took place. If a rider contacts the wrong council, UK licensing authorities are expected to redirect them to the appropriate one.

# *Disclosure of disciplinary actions taken against the driver*

Any disciplinary action taken in relation to a driver is also personal data and should not be shared with the rider. As this case does not amount to a crisis situation and there appear to be no specific actions taken against the driver, no further elaboration is needed.

# *Recommended response to the rider*

Dear [Name],

After carefully reviewing your request for the name of the licensing authority that issued the driver’s Private Hire license and details of any disciplinary actions taken in relation to the driver, we must inform you that we cannot provide this information. The information you requested concerns the driver and does not form part of the personal data that Bolt processes about you. Disclosing it would therefore involve sharing another individual’s personal data to a third party, which we are not permitted to do under Article 15(4) UK GDPR.

Please note that this does not affect your ability to raise complaints. As already communicated, we have reviewed your report in line with our internal processes and taken the appropriate steps. In addition, should you choose to contact the licensing authority responsible for the area where the trip took place, and the matter falls under another authority’s remit, they should redirect your complaint accordingly.

Yours sincerely,
Bolt

To obtain such consent, the person making the call should make clear that the driver lead is consenting to follow-up emails/messages about FATII and Pick and ask the driver lead to verbally consent to this; we should then also clearly maintain records of such consent somewhere on our systems (in case we need to rely on it / use it as evidence on the future) 💡 Again, it would be helpful to see a copy of the call script to confirm that this is being done properly.

Hello [~accountid:712020:793bd952-a372-4264-98c5-05f34ecedce8].

After analysis by the Legal Team of the Tenders Documents provided, it was verified that *the Tender is not suited for Bolt Business model*, as the awarded entity is posed as the *transportation services provider* and the tender establishes +direct control over drivers and requirements for technical quality, availability of service+, etc.

As for *liability of the subcontractor*, the tender documents do not establish specific requirements, instead they *point to Spanish Public Procurement Law, which predicts that the main contractor (in this case, MZ) is fully liable before the contracting authority*.

However, Spanish PP Law states that t*he contracting authority will vet if the subcontractor has capacity/solvency to fulfill the tender requirements*. Hence +why MZ wants Bolt to sign the capacity/solvency documents and declarations - to demonstrate this compliance to the contracting authority, as this is a legally mandatory requirement+ (that Bolt must be able to fulfill the criteria of the tender to be a subcontractor).

+Although the contracting entity does not seem to be able to impose to Bolt any penalties or liability under the contract and the tender specifics or even under Spanish PP law+, the possibility remains that Bolt could still face some sort of *civil liability for knowingly entering into a tender that is not compliant with, as a subcontractor*, and whose requirements cannot be guaranteed.Spanish PP Law establishes sanctions if this happens, but only to the awarded entity (MZ): termination of the contract and financial penalties of up to 50% of the amount of the subcontract.

If the Business Team decides to move forward, the *approach recommended by the Legal Team is not to formally appear as subcontractor towards the contracting entity, under MZ’s public contract. Hence, do not sign any of the documents/declarations*. Bolt could still enter into a contract with MZ, in Bolt’s standard terms, only providing platform access.

However, *this option still carries considerable risks*, since +it seems unlikely that the contracting entity would not know or have visibility that it’s Bolt providing the service+ as subcontractor, and +could accuse MZ of legal and tender breach, potentially leading to termination of the awarded contract+, and *exposing Bolt to liability towards MZ*, which amount cannot be certainly determined but could amount to the value of the awarded contract.

If the *Business Team chooses to sign the capacity/solvency documents and declarations*, +Bolt would be formally introduced as subcontractor towards the contracting entity+, meaning *Bolt would commit to tender criteria that are not aligned with the Bolt’s Business model, which carries major risk and potencial liability, since Bolt cannot guarantee the tender requirements*.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:61447d4ac2fda2006a972cbb] The Transport General Authority (TGA) has issued a compliance notice requiring all ride-hailing platforms to display the Trip ID (Order ID) on all rider invoices and within the trip information shown to passengers during the trip.

I believe we should *prioritize this implementation* because:

* *Non-compliance will trigger fines* for each operating partner until the feature is live.
* *License renewal is approaching*, and TGA has indicated that failure to meet this requirement may directly affect renewal or even lead to suspension.
* This requirement applies to *all platforms*, so ensuring early compliance protects us from unnecessary regulatory and operational risk.

Given the potential financial and licensing consequences, I recommend treating this as a *high-urgency regulatory item*. Is this a very difficult feature to implement? 

Let me know if you need more context or want to have a call discuss next steps.

Hello Mariana, Beatriz, and Legal Team,

Thanks for the detailed analysis and for the recommendations provided but we still need to have a more thorough risk assessment from your side.

There are a few points I would like to clarify to be able to properly assess the business decision here:

----

h3. *1. Liability – direct vs indirect exposure*

You mention that the tender does not establish liability for the subcontractor (Bolt) and that Spanish Public Procurement Law places full liability on the awarded entity (in this case, Mobility Zeus).
Based on this, my understanding is that *Bolt would not be directly liable before the contracting authority*.

Could you please confirm explicitly whether this interpretation is correct?

----

h3. *2. Nature of Bolt’s potential exposure*

You also mention the possibility of Bolt facing *civil liability* for “knowingly entering into a tender that is not compliant” with our model.

To understand the risk level:

* *What specific civil liabilities or penalties could Bolt realistically face?*
* *Are we talking about administrative fines, damages claimed by MZ, or something else?*
* *What would be the financial magnitude we should assume?* (e.g., thousands, hundreds of thousands, proportional to contract size, etc.)
* *What is the probability of such a liability being triggered?*

We need to understand this in order to weigh potential gains vs. potential losses.

----

h3. *3. Structural impact on our B2G strategy*

From your assessment, I understand that the key misalignment with this tender is that it requires the awarded entity (and by extension, any subcontractor) to:

* Exercise *direct control over drivers*;
* Commit to *technical quality standards*;
* Guarantee *availability of service* in terms that are not fully compatible with the Bolt Business platform model.

My concern is that these types of requirements are *not unique to this specific tender*. From what we are seeing in the market, *most, if not all, public tenders in this space contain very similar clauses* around direct control, quality, and availability.

At the same time, Bolt is in the process of *building a specific B2G strategy*, including *dedicated headcount and a new department* precisely so that we can start *competing for these public tenders*, whether as main contractor or as subcontractor.

This leads to a key question I need your help to clarify:

* *If these requirements (driver control, technical quality, availability, etc.) are structurally present in almost all tenders, does this mean that Bolt will* *_never_* *be in a position to be fully compliant from a strict legal perspective?*
* If the answer is yes, *does it follow that any B2G activity will always entail an “assessed risk” scenario*, where we knowingly operate in a model that is not 100% aligned with the wording of the tender but is accepted as a calculated business risk?

In other words:

{quote}*Are we essentially saying that the situation we face with this tender (MZ) is not an exception, but the “new normal” for any B2G opportunity involving public transportation tenders in Spain?*{quote}

If so, it is important for us to have a *clear, principled position* on how Bolt wants to approach these tenders going forward (e.g. “never participate where these conditions exist” vs. “participate with a defined risk framework and internal guidelines”).

----

h3. *4. Risk allocation between Bolt and Mobility Zeus*

Since the main exposure appears to be through our *commercial relationship with Mobility Zeus*, not directly with the contracting authority:

* *Can Bolt negotiate a contractual safeguard with MZ* that limits or excludes our liability in case the tender is terminated by the contracting authority?
* *What form could such a safeguard take?* (e.g. limitation of liability clause, indemnification, no-fault termination, etc.)
* *Would such an agreement materially reduce Bolt’s exposure?*

This is important because if Bolt can contractually protect itself vis-à-vis MZ, the residual risk might become acceptable.

----

h3. *5. Need for a quantified view to make a decision*

We are facing a *hard deadline on November 30*.
This tender represents *~450k€ of incremental yearly revenue*, which is extremely significant for Bolt Business Spain.

To make the decision, we urgently need:

* A *clear articulation of the real risks to Bolt*;
* A *quantified estimate of potential financial exposure*;
* Confirmation on whether contractual protections with MZ could sufficiently mitigate these risks.

----

Thanks for prioritizing this. *Given the strategic relevance and the proximity of the deadline, we need these clarifications as a matter of urgency so we can unlock a decision.*

I’ve reviewed the draft lease and have set out the key points I recommend we negotiate and sense-check internally, as you may be comfortable with some of these risks given the low monthly cost and intended unmanned use.

# *Break Right*

The lease is a fixed 12-month term with no ability for us to exit early. I suggest requesting a tenant break option (e.g., after 3 or 6 months on one month’s notice). Please let me know if full lock-in is acceptable to you.

# *Repairing & Reinstatement Obligations (Clauses 3.3.1, 3.15.1–3.15.2)*

The lease requires full internal repair and decoration, reinstatement at end of term and payment of all landlord costs if we miss anything. For a small unmanned office, I recommend:

* adding a Schedule of Condition;
* removing the redecoration obligation;
* limiting reinstatement to alterations we actually make.

However, let me know if you’re happy taking broader dilapidations exposure given the low rent.

# *Indemnity (Clause 3.14)*

There is a very broad, uncapped indemnity in favour of the landlord (covers all costs “directly or indirectly”). I suggest narrowing this to only losses caused directly by our negligence or breach.

# *Payment Terms (Clause 1.3.5)*

All charges must be paid within 7 days. I recommend extending this to 14 days unless you’re happy with the shorter timeframe.

# *Payment Method (Clause 3.1.1(a)(ii))*

The landlord can require payment by standing order. If this doesn’t work for finance, we should amend to only allow bank transfer or any reasonable method - please confirm.

# *Default Interest (Interest definition)*

Interest is 4% above NatWest base rate. Market is usually lower. I propose asking for 2% above base.

# *Service Charge*

The service charge (£97) is uncapped and not itemised. We may want to request clarification and/or an annual cap. Please confirm if you are comfortable with it as-is.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

From :gemini: 💪 on this [paper|https://arxiv.org/html/2205.02274v4]

This is a highly relevant paper for a Technical PM in ride-hailing. It proposes a method to estimate *Global Treatment Effects* (what happens if you roll a feature out to everyone) using standard user-split A/B tests, while mathematically removing the bias caused by supply constraints (interference).

Here is a summary of the concept, the technical assumptions required to use it, and how you can validate them with your engineering team.



h3. *1. The Core Concept: Shadow Price (SP) Estimator*



The Problem: Marketplace Interference

In a ride-hailing marketplace, standard A/B tests (RCTs) are biased. If you give a discount to the Treatment Group, they book more rides. This consumes the finite supply of drivers, leaving fewer cars for the Control Group. This makes the Control Group perform worse than normal, artificially inflating the "lift" of your experiment. The paper proves that the standard RCT estimator always overestimates the global treatment effect in these settings1.

The Solution: Using Shadow Prices

Instead of comparing the total/average value captured by Treatment vs. Control (which is the standard approach), the authors propose comparing the marginal value captured by each group2.

* *How it works:* Ride-hailing platforms match supply and demand using optimization algorithms (Linear Programs). These algorithms produce "Shadow Prices" (Dual Variables)—a mathematical output representing the incremental value of having _one more_ unit of supply or demand^3^.

* *The Estimator:* The Shadow Price (SP) Estimator calculates the treatment effect by looking at the shadow prices associated with the users in your experiment. It effectively "linearizes" the value function correctly, accounting for the fact that supply is limited^4^.

* 
*The Result:* This method yields an estimate that is significantly less biased than a standard A/B test and does not require the operational complexity of Switchback (time-split) testing^5555^.


----



h3. *2. Key Assumptions & Technical Requirements*



For this method to work in your specific context, the following assumptions must hold true.



h4. *A. Your Matching is Optimization-Based*



The methodology relies on the platform matching supply and demand via a "generalized matching" algorithm (like a Linear Program or Network Flow) rather than decentralized customer choice (like Airbnb) or simple greedy heuristics^6^.



* 
*Why:* You need the algorithm to generate the "dual data" (shadow prices) mathematically^7^.




h4. *B. "Blind" Matching Assumption*



The matching algorithm must treat a user the same way regardless of whether they are in Treatment or Control. The treatment can change the _arrival rate_ (probability of requesting), but once a request is made, the algorithm must see them as interchangeable^8888^.



* *Why:* If the matching logic prioritizes Treatment users _because_ they are Treatment users, the shadow prices become distorted.



h4. *C. Access to Dual Data*



Your experimentation infrastructure needs access to the outcome of the matching solve—specifically the "dual solution" (shadow prices), not just the "primal solution" (who matched with whom)^9^.



* 
*Why:* The estimator formula requires $A^{\tau, experiment}$ (the shadow price of a demand unit)^10^.




h4. *D. Sign-Consistency (Preferred)*



The treatment effect should generally move in one direction across user types (e.g., the discount doesn't increase rides for X while decreasing rides for Y)^11111111^.



* *Why:* While not strictly fatal, the bias reduction guarantees are strongest when the treatment effect is consistent.

----



h3. *3. How to Check These Assumptions (Action Plan)*



Here are the specific questions to ask your Data Science and Engineering counterparts to see if this method is viable for your team:

|*Assumption*|*Question for Engineering/DS*|*Success Criteria*|
|*Optimization-Based*|"Is our dispatch/matching logic solved using a Linear Program (LP) or Min-Cost Flow solver (like Gurobi, CPLEX, or custom), or is it a greedy heuristic?"|You need an LP-based solver. If it's a greedy heuristic (e.g., "closest driver"), this math does not apply directly.|
|*Dual Data Access*|"Do we currently log the 'dual variables' or 'shadow prices' from the matching solver? If not, how expensive would it be to log them?"|You need the {{dual}} values associated with the demand constraints in the LP^12^.|
|*Blind Matching*|"Does the experiment flag pass into the matching objective function? Or does it only affect the user's decision to request?"|You want the matching algorithm to be *unaware* of the user's experiment bucket.|
|*Secondary Metrics*|"Do we optimize for a secondary metric (like ETA or Green Rides)?"|The paper provides a method to derive "secondary shadow prices" using complementary slackness if you care about metrics other than the main objective^13^.|



h3. *4. Summary for Stakeholders*



If you need to pitch this to leadership, here is the summary:

{quote}"Our current A/B tests likely overestimate the value of our features because they don't account for how treated users 'cannibalize' the available drivers. By logging a specific mathematical output from our matching engine (shadow prices), we can mathematically correct this bias. This allows us to run standard A/B tests—which are faster and more granular than Switchback tests—while still getting an accurate read on the global impact."{quote}

*Would you like me to help you draft the technical query for your engineering team, or explain the math behind the "Secondary Estimators" (Appendix A) if your team tracks metrics like ETA or cancellation rates?*

+*UPDATE (27.11)*+

* Questions have been put to the business, as well as Regional Legal, which will determine final privacy advice. Not much point giving the advice yet, as Q&A responses may mean that it needs to be tweaked. I have chased Shrishti for responses.
* In the meantime, saving the key points as an internal comment here, in case they need to be relayed next week to the business while I am OOO (NB. this is based on EU-wide privacy analysis [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14CmJpL-aSKQ82zKFbWsw_Xszjh9uzeEkOMkxvRd3gzI/edit?tab=t.0]).
* NB. This is for the UK only. The business seems to be launching this in several countries, but this is the only country we have been looped in for so far. I have flagged that we should be added to other countries when needed.

----

*KEY ISSUES / MITIGATIONS:*

* *Transparency*: Driver-facing articles / transparency materials ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.c383kapuni8h]) need to be more transparent on: (i) what KPIs Bolt is monitoring, and why these are necessary; (ii) how drivers will be warned about exclusion (and how exclusion will only be from the categories, not rides altogether). In the long term, the Privacy Team should also consider updates to the driver privacy notice.
* *Warning/exclusion comms*: These comms ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.4ntyngmbuskj]) should be clear on: (i) which KPIs have not been met (and if possible, the threshold that has not been met); and (ii) clear information on how to appeal. Currently, the level of detail could be better. I am speaking with stakeholders about this via comments in the docs themselves, which is ongoing.
* *Automations*: If the process for monitoring, excluding and reinstating drivers is entirely automated, then (even though this falls below the A22 threshold) we should ensure that: (i) there is a clearly structured appeal / CS process incorporating human review; (ii) this process is documented internally in a clear way; and (iii) the system is sufficiently robust to minimise the risk of errors.
* *High-risk profiling*: Acceptance rate is a potential KPI for the UK. This is more sensitive than driver rating, finished orders and completion rate, and may amount to disproportionate monitoring of drivers. Given that the UK is a sensitive market, my recommendation is to not use acceptance rate as a KPI. The Privacy Team should also complete a DPIA (this has not yet been done).
* *Photo submissions*: Drivers will be regularly submitting photos of their vehicles for quality check purposes. The current plan seems to be that we will be storing these photos on Sharepoint.  We should: (i) encourage drivers to not include any unnecessary data in the photos; and (ii) ensure that Sharepoint is sufficiently secure / integrated to keep the photos safe and extractable should we need them to respond to DSARs.

{code:python}You are an AI assistant designed to label payout- and Early Cashout-related support tickets. Each ticket is represented with a row in the dataframe {tickets_df} that has the following structure:
        - The first column is the ticket date
        - The second column is the ticket ID
        - The third column is the ticket content
                
    Your task is to carefully read each ticket (row) and decide whether this a complaint or other (for example, a question, a request, or an inquiry). You should only reply with one label per ticket: either "complaint" or "other". 
        
    A complaint describes a problem: the partner has not received a payout, received less money than expected, or the payout is delayed. Complaints are often emotional and use strong language, the partner is articulating their dissatisfaction. Other includes questions, inquiries, or requests, for example regarding access to the feature or changing bank details, and normally use calm and neutral language.

    -------------------

    Examples:
            
    "Good evening, you promised €5.80 for the order, but I was paid €2.60." - the partner is complaining that they received less money than expected, put the label "complaint"

    "Hi, I just recived my paycheck for the previouse week. Do I need to pay the amount myself to you guys or I dont need to pay myself but you take the money from my account?" - the partner is asking whether he should pay the invoice, put the label "other"

    "I need help with my payout. Please change my account number to EE 172200221092769963." - the partner asks to change their bank account number, put "other"

    -------------

    Sometimes a ticket may include several issues, both complaints and questions/requests. In this case, please label the very first issue mentioned by the partner, and ignore the rest of them.
            
    Please use only one of two possible labels, either "complaint" or other". Your reply should include the label only.

    Please format your reply as a python dictionary where the key is the the ticket ID (taken from the second column) and the value is the label: complaint or other. The ID should be formatted as a bigint, and the label should be formatted as a string.{code}

From :gemini: on this [paper|https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.06580]:

This is a highly relevant paper for a Technical PM in ride-hailing. It proposes a method to estimate *Global Treatment Effects* (what happens if you roll a feature out to everyone) using standard user-split A/B tests, while mathematically removing the bias caused by supply constraints (interference).

Here is a summary of the concept, the technical assumptions required to use it, and how you can validate them with your engineering team.



h3. *1. The Core Concept: Shadow Price (SP) Estimator*



The Problem: Marketplace Interference

In a ride-hailing marketplace, standard A/B tests (RCTs) are biased. If you give a discount to the Treatment Group, they book more rides. This consumes the finite supply of drivers, leaving fewer cars for the Control Group. This makes the Control Group perform worse than normal, artificially inflating the "lift" of your experiment. The paper proves that the standard RCT estimator always overestimates the global treatment effect in these settings1.

The Solution: Using Shadow Prices

Instead of comparing the total/average value captured by Treatment vs. Control (which is the standard approach), the authors propose comparing the marginal value captured by each group2.

* *How it works:* Ride-hailing platforms match supply and demand using optimization algorithms (Linear Programs). These algorithms produce "Shadow Prices" (Dual Variables)—a mathematical output representing the incremental value of having _one more_ unit of supply or demand^3^.

* *The Estimator:* The Shadow Price (SP) Estimator calculates the treatment effect by looking at the shadow prices associated with the users in your experiment. It effectively "linearizes" the value function correctly, accounting for the fact that supply is limited^4^.

* 
*The Result:* This method yields an estimate that is significantly less biased than a standard A/B test and does not require the operational complexity of Switchback (time-split) testing^5555^.


----



h3. *2. Key Assumptions & Technical Requirements*



For this method to work in your specific context, the following assumptions must hold true.



h4. *A. Your Matching is Optimization-Based*



The methodology relies on the platform matching supply and demand via a "generalized matching" algorithm (like a Linear Program or Network Flow) rather than decentralized customer choice (like Airbnb) or simple greedy heuristics^6^.



* 
*Why:* You need the algorithm to generate the "dual data" (shadow prices) mathematically^7^.




h4. *B. "Blind" Matching Assumption*



The matching algorithm must treat a user the same way regardless of whether they are in Treatment or Control. The treatment can change the _arrival rate_ (probability of requesting), but once a request is made, the algorithm must see them as interchangeable^8888^.



* *Why:* If the matching logic prioritizes Treatment users _because_ they are Treatment users, the shadow prices become distorted.



h4. *C. Access to Dual Data*



Your experimentation infrastructure needs access to the outcome of the matching solve—specifically the "dual solution" (shadow prices), not just the "primal solution" (who matched with whom)^9^.



* 
*Why:* The estimator formula requires $A^{\tau, experiment}$ (the shadow price of a demand unit)^10^.




h4. *D. Sign-Consistency (Preferred)*



The treatment effect should generally move in one direction across user types (e.g., the discount doesn't increase rides for X while decreasing rides for Y)^11111111^.



* *Why:* While not strictly fatal, the bias reduction guarantees are strongest when the treatment effect is consistent.

----



h3. *3. How to Check These Assumptions (Action Plan)*



Here are the specific questions to ask your Data Science and Engineering counterparts to see if this method is viable for your team:

|*Assumption*|*Question for Engineering/DS*|*Success Criteria*|
|*Optimization-Based*|"Is our dispatch/matching logic solved using a Linear Program (LP) or Min-Cost Flow solver (like Gurobi, CPLEX, or custom), or is it a greedy heuristic?"|You need an LP-based solver. If it's a greedy heuristic (e.g., "closest driver"), this math does not apply directly.|
|*Dual Data Access*|"Do we currently log the 'dual variables' or 'shadow prices' from the matching solver? If not, how expensive would it be to log them?"|You need the {{dual}} values associated with the demand constraints in the LP^12^.|
|*Blind Matching*|"Does the experiment flag pass into the matching objective function? Or does it only affect the user's decision to request?"|You want the matching algorithm to be *unaware* of the user's experiment bucket.|
|*Secondary Metrics*|"Do we optimize for a secondary metric (like ETA or Green Rides)?"|The paper provides a method to derive "secondary shadow prices" using complementary slackness if you care about metrics other than the main objective^13^.|



h3. *4. Summary for Stakeholders*



If you need to pitch this to leadership, here is the summary:

{quote}"Our current A/B tests likely overestimate the value of our features because they don't account for how treated users 'cannibalize' the available drivers. By logging a specific mathematical output from our matching engine (shadow prices), we can mathematically correct this bias. This allows us to run standard A/B tests—which are faster and more granular than Switchback tests—while still getting an accurate read on the global impact."{quote}

*Would you like me to help you draft the technical query for your engineering team, or explain the math behind the "Secondary Estimators" (Appendix A) if your team tracks metrics like ETA or cancellation rates?*
