Commission that driver had to pay is 

{quote}*Commission = expense_cash_commission* + *expense_commission* (48.50 EUR + 190.83 EUR) = €239.33 EUR{quote}

this commission is ±20% of the amount driver had in Ride fees

{quote}Fees = *earning_in_app_ride_fee* + *earning_cash_ride_fee*  (947.70 EUR + 242.50 EUR) = €1,190.20 EUR

Commission % = commission / fees = €239.33 EUR / 1,190.20 EUR = 0.20 = 20%{quote}

the invoice was issued for less than 239.33 because we do *commission netting* in Estonia. 

{quote}*What is Commission Netting?*

*Commission netting* is a process used to simplify how drivers are invoiced for commissions, especially when there are bonuses, campaigns, or compensations involved.

*Without Netting:*

* Normally, a driver would receive separate invoices:
** One for the commission they owe (e.g., 20% of ride fees)
** Separate invoices for any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations they receive

*With Netting (as done in Estonia):*

* Instead of issuing multiple invoices, the system *reduces the commission amount* by the total value of any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations the driver earned.
* The driver receives a *single, lower commission invoice* that already accounts for these discounts.{quote}

You can see discounts earned via cash and app rides in *earning_cash_discount_netted* and *earning_in_app_discount_netted.*

So we can calculate the final netted commission like this:

{quote}Netted Commission = Commission - *earning_cash_discount_netted - earning_in_app_discount_netted* = €239.33 - 26.70 EUR - 79.70 EUR = €132.93{quote}

132.93 is the same amount you can see on Monthly invoice (take invoice from October from [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients/128179276?tab=partner_invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])

h2. Why WebView Caching Was Not Implemented for Bolt+ Subscription Page

h3. *Core Issue - Correct Understanding:*

* *Stack Used*: {{@react-navigation/native-stack}} v6.9.12 with {{react-native-screens}}
* *Actual Behavior*: Screens *DO get remounted* when navigating forward to them (e.g., {{navigation.navigate('Subscription')}})
* *Only preserved*: When using back navigation (e.g., {{navigation.goBack()}})
* *Result*: Each forward navigation to the Subscription screen = full component remount = WebView reload

h3. Solutions Considered and Reasons for Non-Implementation:

h4. 1. *No Navigator Options Available to Prevent Remounting*

*Considered:* Using built-in navigator options to keep screens mounted across forward navigations

*Why not implemented:*

* {{detachInactiveScreens}} - Only exists in {{@react-navigation/stack}} ([JS Stack|https://reactnavigation.org/docs/6.x/stack-navigator/#detachinactivescreens]), *NOT* in {{@react-navigation/native-stack}} [1]
* {{unmountOnBlur}} - Only exists in Tab/Drawer navigators, not any Stack navigator [2]
* *Native Stack Navigator fundamentally remounts screens on forward navigation* - this is inherent behavior with no opt-out option

----

h4. 2. *Moving WebView to Always-Mounted Global Component (Anti-Pattern)*

*Considered:* Create a global WebView instance that stays mounted in a modal/portal, hidden when not in use

*Why not implemented:*

* *Anti-pattern* causing:
* *Memory leaks*: WebView instances consume 20-40MB+ RAM with active JavaScript context
* *Performance degradation*: Hidden WebViews continue executing JavaScript and consuming CPU
* *State management complexity*: Requires complex synchronization between navigation state and WebView visibility
* *Maintenance burden*: Difficult to debug and reason about
* React Native best practices recommend unmounting unused components, not hiding them

----

h4. 3. *Custom Caching with Stale Data Risks*

*Considered:* Implement custom caching mechanism to store/restore WebView state

*Why not implemented:*

* _We can’t cache the data within a WebView, yes, we could technically cache an HTML code, but can’t save the whole web app locally_
_Even if we would’ve achieved this, we would’ve ended up with these issues (_*_which also apply to solution 2_*_):_
* *Cannot reliably know when to refresh* across all edge cases:
* User purchases/cancels subscription in another Bolt app
* Subscription expires or payment fails
* Promotional offers change
* Price updates on server
* Payment method issues
* Server-side configuration changes
* *Complex invalidation logic* required for:
* Time-based expiration (TTL)
* Event-based invalidation
* Cross-app synchronization
* *High risk of showing stale data* = user confusion and support tickets

----

h4. 4. *WebView* {{cacheEnabled}} *Prop [3]*

*Considered:* Using WebView's {{cacheEnabled}} prop

*Why not implemented:*

* {{cacheEnabled}} serves a *completely different purpose*: HTTP-level browser resource caching (images, CSS, JS files)
* *Does NOT*:
* Prevent component remounting on forward navigation
* Preserve WebView JavaScript state
* Cache the subscription page data/state
* Only affects how the WebView fetches web resources, not the React component lifecycle



h3. References:

# [Native Stack Navigator Documentation|https://reactnavigation.org/docs/6.x/stack-navigator/#detachinactivescreens]
# [JS Stack `detachInactiveScreens` Option|https://reactnavigation.org/docs/6.x/stack-navigator/#detachinactivescreens]
# [WebView `cacheEnabled` Explanation|https://github.com/react-native-webview/react-native-webview/blob/master/docs/Reference.md#cacheenabled]

Hi [~accountid:712020:5b77edca-b761-46b2-8328-76ff4b4d0563] 

The NZ law does not prescribe a single format, consent must be *evidenced in a durable, auditable form*—especially when the processing is optional and involves a non-essential use of personal information.

h4. *1. Phone call + follow-up email*

A phone call alone is *not sufficient*, as it does not create a verifiable consent record.
However, *if the driver provides written confirmation in response to the follow-up email*, that is acceptable.

* Phone call: can be used to explain the request.
* *Consent must be captured in writing* (e.g., replying “Yes, I agree”) so that we have clear evidence.

h4. *2. In-app chat conversation*

Yes—*this is absolutely sufficient*, provided the driver gives an unambiguous written confirmation in the chat (e.g., “Yes, I consent to my photo being used for the leaderboard”).

The in-app channel creates a durable record, which meets compliance expectations.

----

h3. Message that can be used to request consent:

{quote}_Hi [Driver Name], we’d love your permission to use your driver photo for [leaderboard feature]._

_Just reply to confirm your consent. You can withdraw it anytime by contacting us through the app or at [Local Ops Email], and we’ll stop using your photo from then on._

_Are you happy for us to include your photo?_{quote}

# +*Manual dispatching of Meet & Greet orders to Odysse*+

* *Data protection:* Low. Odysse already receives the relevant allocation and driver data through existing fleet integrations.

*Question for @Thomas:*

# +*Priority access for Odysse drivers to pre-booked airport orders*+

*Overall legal risk: Primarily reputational/business rather than legal risk*

* No competition-law concerns identified.
* Main risk area is perception of fairness among non-fleet drivers - [~accountid:5d9c300987dd6f0dcb4d2b58] please confirm that the business is ok accepting this potential risk.
* Mitigations include transparent logic, internal record-keeping, and clearly framing priority access as necessary for reliability on time-critical airport transfers.

*Question for @Georgia:*
→ From a public policy and regulatory standpoint, would prioritising fleet drivers (without excluding other drivers) raise any concerns with regulators or licensing authorities?

*Question for @Thomas:*
→ Does surfacing jobs earlier to Odysse drivers affect our data processing responsibilities or require any privacy-related changes?

Design doc from :gemini: : 

h1. Design Doc: AI Scorecard Summarizer Service

Author: [Your Name/Team]

Status: Draft

Date: 2025-05-20

h2. 1. Executive Summary

The Experimentation Platform currently provides raw quantitative data (metrics, deltas, p-values). However, experimenters spend significant time manually synthesizing these numbers with the original hypothesis found in external documentation (Confluence/Google Docs) to create a "Scorecard" narrative.

This document proposes the *AI Scorecard Summarizer*, a backend service that automates the generation of this narrative. It utilizes an LLM to synthesize the _Qualitative Context_ (from feature specs) and the _Quantitative Result_ (from experiment metrics) into a human-readable summary.

h2. 2. Goals & Non-Goals

h3. Goals

* *Contextual Analysis:* Automatically ingest and parse text from linked Confluence pages or Google Docs.
* *Statistical Interpretation:* Translate raw JSON metric results into natural language findings (e.g., "statistically significant lift in conversion").
* *Draft Generation:* Produce a structured Markdown summary (Hypothesis, Results, Conclusion) in under 15 seconds.
* *Human-in-the-loop:* Ensure the generated summary is editable before being published to the permanent scorecard.

h3. Non-Goals

* *Decision Making:* The AI will not declare a "Ship/No-Ship" decision; it only summarizes facts.
* *Image Parsing:* The system will not interpret screenshots or diagrams within the linked documents (text only).

h2. 3. High-Level Architecture

The system consists of three main stages: *Ingestion*, *Synthesis*, and *Presentation*.

{noformat}sequenceDiagram
    participant User as Experimenter (UI)
    participant XP as XP Platform (Backend)
    participant Doc as Doc Scraper Service
    participant LLM as LLM Gateway
    participant DB as Database

    User->>XP: Click "Generate AI Summary" (provides Doc URL)
    XP->>Doc: Request content (Confluence/GDoc URL)
    Doc-->>XP: Return sanitized plain text
    XP->>XP: Fetch Experiment JSON (Metrics)
    XP->>XP: Construct Contextual Prompt
    XP->>LLM: Send Prompt (Context + JSON)
    LLM-->>XP: Return Structured Summary (Markdown)
    XP-->>User: Display Draft in Editor
    User->>XP: Edit & Save
    XP->>DB: Persist Scorecard

{noformat}

h2. 4. Detailed Component Design

h3. 4.1. The Document Ingestion Layer ("The Reader")

We need a service to fetch the "Feature Context."

* *Input:* URL (Confluence or Google Doc).
* *Connectors:*
** _Confluence:_ Use Atlassian REST API ({{/wiki/rest/api/content}}).
** _Google Docs:_ Use Google Drive/Docs API.
* *Preprocessing:*
** Convert HTML to Plain Text.
** Remove boilerplate (headers, footers, sidebars).
** *Truncation:* If the document exceeds 15k tokens, we perform a "compression" pass (ask LLM to summarize the doc first) or truncate the middle.

h3. 4.2. The Metric Parser ("The Translator")

Raw JSON is token-heavy and hard for LLMs to read accurately. We must flatten the JSON before sending.

* *Raw JSON:*
{noformat}{
  "metric_id": "checkout_conversion",
  "control_mean": 0.05,
  "treatment_mean": 0.055,
  "delta_relative": 0.10,
  "p_value": 0.03,
  "confidence_interval": [0.01, 0.19]
}

{noformat}
* Prompt-Ready String:
"Metric: Checkout Conversion. Control: 5.0%. Variant: 5.5%. Delta: +10% (Significant, p=0.03)."

h3. 4.3. The Prompt Strategy

We will use a *Chain-of-Thought* approach to prevent the LLM from hallucinating math.

*System Prompt:*

{quote}You are a senior data scientist. Your job is to write an experiment report. You rely STRICTLY on the provided metric data for numbers. Do not calculate new stats. Use the provided Document Context to explain _why_ we ran the test.{quote}

*User Prompt Structure:*

# *Context (The 'Why'):* [Insert scraped text from Confluence/GDoc]
# *Results (The 'What'):* [Insert Pre-processed Metrics List]
#* _Instruction:_ Group metrics by "Primary", "Secondary", and "Guardrail". Highlight only statistically significant changes.
# *Task:* Write a scorecard summary in the following format:
#* *Hypothesis:* (1 sentence summary from Context)
#* *Key Findings:* (Bulleted list of significant metric movements)
#* *Analysis:* (Connect the Hypothesis to the Findings. Did the feature work as intended?)

h2. 5. Data Flow & Storage

# *Trigger:* User clicks "Generate" on the Experiment Result page.
# *Payload Construction:* Backend aggregates {{experiment_metadata}}, {{metric_results_json}}, and {{external_doc_text}}.
# *LLM Interaction:* Call internal LLM (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, or Llama 3) with temperature {{0.3}} (low creativity, high factual adherence).
# *Draft Storage:* The result is *not* immediately saved as the final report. It is sent to the frontend state.
# *Final Save:* The user modifies the text in a Markdown editor and hits "Publish." Only then is it written to the {{experiment_scorecards}} table.

h2. 6. Security & Privacy

* *PII Redaction:* The Document Ingestion Layer must run a regex pass to mask emails or specific user IDs found in design docs before sending to the LLM.
* *Access Control (ACLs):*
** The service needs a "Service Account" to read Confluence/GDocs.
** We must ensure the user triggering the generation actually has permission to view the linked design doc. We can implement an "On-Behalf-Of" flow or verify the user's email against the doc's ACLs.
* *Data Retention:* The LLM provider (if external) must have a zero-retention policy.

h2. 7. Risks & Mitigation

|*Risk*|*Mitigation*|
|*Hallucination* (AI invents numbers)|# Pass pre-calculated significance flags in the prompt.
\\
# Add specific system instruction: "If a metric is not in the JSON, do not mention it."|
|*Context Window Overflow* (Doc too long)|Implement a "Map-Reduce" strategy: Summarize the design doc first, then pass the summary to the final generation prompt.|
|*Broken Links/Permissions*|Graceful error handling in UI: "Unable to access Confluence doc. Generating report based on metrics only."|
|*Latency*|Show a skeleton loader with a specific "Analyzing metrics..." and "Reading documentation..." progress stepper.|

h2. 8. Development Phases

# *Phase 1 (MVP):* Manual copy-paste of context text (no API scraping). Full metrics parsing. Simple summary generation.
# *Phase 2 (Integration):* Confluence API integration.
# *Phase 3 (Refinement):* GDocs integration and "Regenerate with specific focus" (e.g., "Focus on latency metrics") options.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

# *Weekly changes in fleet debt (fleet_debt)*

There are only two ways to see the debt. We have tables that allow us to see current debt of the fleets by the date of the last activity. We have a model that run periodically and provide us the data of the current debt on a specific date. So we can easily query what is the current debt. 

And for the historical data we do the snapshots once per month of what was this debt. This historic data you can see here for Azerbaijan: [https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/17939?City=&Country=Azerbaijan&Created Month=|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/17939?City=&Country=Azerbaijan&Created%20Month=]

So unfortunately we can’t show you a weekly change in debt. You only can see the current one or the snapshots of the current debt in the previous months as on the dashboards I provided.

I’ve reviewed the counterparty’s proposed changes to the NDA and I’m comfortable accepting all of them except for *two clauses*, for which I’ve suggested alternative wording.

# *Jurisdiction / Dispute Resolution:*
The counterparty proposes resolving disputes through arbitration at the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC). Given the high cost and logistical burden of arbitrating in Singapore—especially for a document as straightforward as an NDA—I’ve proposed using *English law and the Courts of England and Wales* instead. This is a standard, neutral, and far more cost-effective option for cross-border agreements.
# *Mandatory Disclosure Notification:*
They included the wording “*if possible*” in the clause requiring prior notice when disclosure is mandated by law. This creates a broad loophole, as the receiving party could always claim it was “not possible.” I’ve therefore proposed replacing it with *“to the extent permitted by law,”* which is a more precise and widely accepted limitation.

Hi [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] 

Thanks for raising this. From a legal perspective, we do not need to update either the Customer Terms or the Driver Terms ahead of the VAT change on 2 January. The Customer Terms already state that all sums are inclusive of VAT unless stated otherwise, which covers both our current TOMS position and the move to full VAT on the fare.

On the driver side, the current terms also do not need updating. All of our UK drivers are currently not VAT registered, but even if we start working with VAT-registered drivers or fleets in the future, the existing terms already give Bolt enough flexibility to adjust how payouts and invoicing work without needing a contractual amendment. Any changes for VAT-registered drivers would be handled operationally through onboarding flows, invoicing settings and payout calculations rather than in the legal T&Cs.

What we do need to ensure operationally now is that

* the fare displayed in the app includes VAT
* invoices show the correct VAT amount
* rider comms clearly explain the fare breakdown

If these elements are in place, we are covered from a legal perspective.

For any deeper tax or invoicing questions, Tanel is person to advise, as this becomes more of an implementation and tax matter than a legal one. 

Happy to support with any driver/rider comms.

{quote}Dear [Rider Name],Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention. 

We fully understand your concern regarding the presence of a recording device aboard the vehicle during your Bolt ride. 

Please note that drivers using the Bolt platform are independent providers, not Bolt employees. If a driver records or shares a video, they act as an independent _data controller_ under data protection law and are solely responsible for ensuring that any such processing complies with the GDPR and applicable local legislation, including obtaining any required consent. Bolt does not provide, install, or control any recording devices, and we do not have access to or the ability to remove or delete such content ourselves.We provide clear guidance and recommendations to drivers who choose to use recording devices, including the data protection compliance steps they should follow when operating a CCTV device in their vehicle. 

Please note that any requests to access or delete CCTV footage must be directed to the driver, as they are the data controller and have full control over such recordings. While Bolt does not hold or manage this data, we can assist you by transferring your request to the relevant driver if needed.That said, we take reports of this nature very seriously. 

We have escalated the matter internally and will be contacting the Driver to inform them of the situation. We have also reminded them of their obligations under data protection law and the standards expected from drivers using the Bolt platform.We appreciate your feedback, which helps us strengthen our privacy and transparency practices. Bolt is continuously working to improve in-app and in-vehicle notifications so that riders are better informed when recording devices may be in use.We sincerely regret any distress this incident has caused and thank you again for taking the time to alert us. 

Please don’t hesitate to reach out to our customer support team if you have any further questions or concerns.

Sincerely,{quote}

*Before the response is sent Ops will need to ensure it has reached out to the Fleet and directed the Fleet and its Driver to our CCTV Guidelines in TW:* [https://bolt.eu/zh-tw/support/articles/21163/|https://bolt.eu/zh-tw/support/articles/21163/|smart-link] *We have an* {{interim}} *(*{color:#ff5630}*not final*{color}*) template that can be used to contact the Fleet, but I'd suggest that Ops aligns with TW Management on the response to ensure that the tone is acceptable in line with local cultural practices as we don't want to strain the relationship with one of our few Fleet Providers:*

{quote}Dear [*FO Name*],

We are reaching out regarding a privacy concern reported to Bolt involving one of your drivers, {{[Driver's full name]}}, in connection with a ride that took place on {{[ride date]}}.

According to the report, the driver allegedly recorded a passenger without consent, which has caused significant distress to the passenger.We take such matters extremely seriously. As such, we urge you to immediately review this incident and take appropriate action in line with your responsibilities as a data controller. Please also remind the driver involved of their obligations to treat all passengers respectfully and to comply with applicable data protection laws.

As a reminder, Drivers are considered independent data controllers under applicable data protection regulations. This means that Drivers are responsible for ensuring that any recording or sharing of passenger data complies with local data protection legislation, particularly regarding transparency, consent, and lawful processing. If any of your drivers use cameras or other recording devices aboard their vehicle, please ensure that:

* passengers are clearly informed through visible notices that a recording is taking place;
* the purpose, controller details, data retention period, and a reference to a privacy notice are made available; and
* any processing of recordings is conducted lawfully and securely.

We also recommend that you review your internal privacy policies and ensure that they clearly describe how personal data from recordings is processed and protected. Recording customers, especially without consent, constitutes a violation of privacy rights and may have legal consequences.While we provide this guidance, we would like to reiterate that as independent data controllers, you have the autonomy to decide how to act on this advice. However, you remain accountable for ensuring compliance with data protection law and for any breaches arising from your or your drivers’ actions.

Please confirm once you have reviewed the situation and taken the necessary steps in response to this report.If you have any questions or require further clarification, please don’t hesitate to contact us.

Kind regards,{quote}

+*UPDATE (28.11) - Q&A Responses*+

* The only KPIs we would be looking at are Driver Rating and Acceptance Rate (and Driver Score, if applicable).
** Ok. AR is obviously higher-risk and certainly falls within the category of ‘profiling’.
** This is something we can do (per ICO Guidance), but we should flag: (i) AR is higher risk than DR; (ii) we should ensure transparency so that the processing is not invisible;  (iii) we should definitely conduct a DPIA for this (see [here|https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/examples-of-processing-likely-to-result-in-high-risk/]); and (iv) we should ensure we have clear and justifiable reasons for relying on these KPIs (for the sake of fairness) 💡 
** NB. If the individual objects, we can argue compelling overriding grounds.
* Current plan is for exclusions to be manual. In the long term, use of category search filters will mean that the process is automated. The same methodology applies to reinstating the driver.
** Ok - this lowers the privacy risk profile. But we should still make sure that the system is clear, robust, documented and efficiently executed 💡 Otherwise, the bulk of my advice here does not change.
* We will be sharing warning comms with the drivers 1-2 days in advance of removal.
** At least 24 hours should be ok ✅ 
* Regarding reviewing photo submissions, in the short term this will be done by local teams. In the long term, we will embed a tool (in-house/outsourced) in our system.
** Fine. In the long term, if we integrate third-party tools, we may need a DPA to be implemented 💡 
* It is still unclear where mystery shopper feedback will be stored.
** I need to re-ask the business this question (?) 
* Driver amenities are not currently marked on the app / profile for now.
** Ok. If we are not storing it then we are not storing it - processing less data means fewer privacy concerns. As long as this does not create operational concerns, then fine from my POV ✅

+*UPDATED ANALYSIS*+

* Central Privacy Assessment has been updated: [LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14CmJpL-aSKQ82zKFbWsw_Xszjh9uzeEkOMkxvRd3gzI/edit?tab=t.0]
* Updated issues / mitigations are below. These have been posted on the parent ticket.
** *Transparency*: Driver-facing articles / transparency materials ([+here+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.c383kapuni8h]) need to be more transparent on: (i) what KPIs Bolt is monitoring, and why these are necessary; (ii) how drivers will be warned about exclusion (and how exclusion will only be from the categories, not rides altogether). In the long term, the Privacy Team should also consider updates to the driver privacy notice.
** *Warning/exclusion comms*: These comms ([+here+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.4ntyngmbuskj]) should be clear on: (i) which KPIs have not been met (and if possible, the threshold that has not been met); and (ii) clear information on how to appeal. Currently, the level of detail could be better. I am speaking with stakeholders about this via comments in the docs themselves, which is ongoing.
** *Exclusion / Reinstatement Process*: Currently, this is being done manually, but will be moved to automations in the long term. In both cases, we should ensure that: (i) there is a clearly structured appeal / CS process incorporating human review; (ii) this process is documented internally in a clear way; and (iii) the system is sufficiently robust to minimise the risk of errors.
** *High-risk profiling*: Acceptance rate is a potential KPI for the UK. This is more sensitive than driver rating, and may amount to disproportionate monitoring of drivers. Given that the UK is a sensitive market, my recommendation is to not use acceptance rate as a KPI. The Privacy Team should also complete a DPIA (this has not yet been done).
** *Photo submissions*: Drivers will be regularly submitting photos of their vehicles for quality check purposes. The current plan seems to be that we will be storing these photos on Sharepoint.  We should: (i) encourage drivers to not include any unnecessary data in the photos; and (ii) ensure that Sharepoint is sufficiently secure / integrated to keep the photos safe and extractable should we need them to respond to DSARs. If we rely on any third-party automations in the long term, we should make sure to implement data processing agreements.

From a regulatory perspective, adjusting the surge indicator so that it is not shown below a 1.2x multiplier appears to be acceptable in Ontario. Municipal bylaws require that riders are presented with an upfront fare or fare estimate that incorporates all charges, including any dynamic pricing. However, regulators do not require that dynamic pricing or surcharges be labelled or displayed separately.

Provided that the app continues to show riders a clear, all-in fare before they confirm a trip, removing or adjusting the surge indicator for lower multipliers should not raise compliance or transparency concerns, and (as you have pointed out) it remains consistent with general market practice.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

I reinvestigated it once again and don’t see this problem any more. Used this query:


{noformat}with order_payments as (
	select 
		smoo.id as offer_order_id,
		smoo.offer_id ,
		smoo.target_id,
		cast(json_extract_scalar(smc.bonus_data, '$.value') as double) as discount_value,
		sspo.id as payment_id
	from ng_public.subscription_marketplace_offer_order as smoo
	join ng_public.subscription_marketplace_campaign_usage as smcu on
		smoo.id = smcu.offer_order_id
	join ng_public.subscription_marketplace_campaign as smc	on
		smc.id = smcu.campaign_id 
	join ng_public.subscription_subscription_payment_order as sspo on
		smoo.order_id = sspo.subscription_id 
	where smoo.state = 'cancellation_requested'
)
select 
	offer_order_id,
	offer_id,
	target_id,
	sum(discount_value) = 0 as is_trial,
	count(payment_id) as number_of_payments
from order_payments
group by 
	offer_order_id,
	offer_id,
	target_id
having
	count(payment_id) = 1 and
	sum(discount_value) = 0
;{noformat}

Thanks [~accountid:712020:0a98abfb-ef42-4b14-8064-5213eb99bdc8] - this is helpful. In which case, my thoughts from the privacy side are below. I otherwise defer to Regional Legal for their own views.

In short - We can {color:#36b37e}*proceed*{color} with this ✅  +*_provided that_*+ +*the below steps are taken*+. The UK is currently a high-risk market in terms of driver monitoring and transparency, and so we need to be extra careful in terms of how we roll this out (e.g., we are currently subject to an inquiry from the UK regulator which touches on some of these themes) ⚠️

Our central privacy assessment on this initiative can be found here ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14CmJpL-aSKQ82zKFbWsw_Xszjh9uzeEkOMkxvRd3gzI/edit?tab=t.0]) which applies to the UK as well as the EU, and which flags the risks and mitigation steps that we need to consider. The key points are as follows (each colour denotes the risk/priority level, with red being the highest):

* 🔴 *Transparency*: 
** The in-app guidance ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.c383kapuni8h]) and driver comms ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.4ntyngmbuskj]) needs to be as explicit and clear as possible on: (i) why Bolt needs to measure KPIs to determine eligibility for premium categories; (ii) which specific KPIs are used to determine eligibility (as well as the thresholds, if the business is willing to share these); (iii) what exclusion means for the drivers in practical terms (i.e., that they will just be excluded from the _categories_, not Bolt as a whole, until they meet the KPIs again); and (iv) where the driver can find more information about data processing (i.e., it should include a link to the UK driver privacy notice). Currently, the materials could be more detailed on these topics.
** We must also ensure that drivers are presented comms in good time about warnings / exclusions and reinstatements, so that we do not open ourselves  up to accusations of ‘shadow exclusion’.
* :orange_circle: *Exclusions / Appeals Process*:
** Both in the case of manual checks and the eventually automated system, we should ensure that: (i) there is a clearly structured customer support process to handle appeals and questions from affected drivers (which incorporates human review); (ii) the process for warnings, exclusions, appeals and reinstatement are clearly documented internally; and (iii) reinstatement to the premium categories should occur once eligibility criteria are met again.
** We should also ensure that any automations are robustly designed to minimise the risk of any system errors.
* :orange_circle: *KPIs*:
** As Driver Score is not active in the UK, I understand that we will be using Acceptance Rate and Driver Rating as the KPIs to determine eligibility.
** Acceptance Rate is higher risk than Driver Rating in this context, as it comes across as more operationally controlling by Bolt and may be regarded as intrusive. As such, the business should carefully consider whether each KPI is *_strictly required_* for the matching logic - if it is, then we should clearly document internally why the KPI is necessary (so that we can rely on this explanation if challenged); if it is not, then it should not be used 
** Our preference would be to rely on Driver Rating rather than Acceptance Rate, but this is ultimately a decision for the local General Manager, and is something that we can do if strictly needed.
* :green_circle: *Photo Submissions (Quality Inspections)*:
** When we ask drivers to submit photos of their vehicles for quality inspections, we should encourage them not to include anything unnecessary in the photos (e.g., their faces / the faces of anyone else, ID cards etc.), so that we are not unintentionally processing any high-risk data.
** To the extent not already completed, InfoSec should assess whether Sharepoint is a sufficiently secure platform for storing driver photo submissions (on the assumption that we will be using this in the UK as well as in the EU). Also, such storage should be structured in such a way that the photos can be easily located, extracted and provided to drivers who have submitted data access requests for the same.
** If the business decides to embed any external tools to review photo submissions manually, the Privacy team should be consulted about entering into a data processing agreement with any relevant third-party providers. We should also ensure that the automations are robustly designed to minimise the risk of system errors.

Happy to discuss if you have any questions about this 🙂

From your logs, I see you run the {{boltml run-train}} separately.

To run it in stand-alone mode you need to provide the arguments (so you need to add {{boltml run-train -L city_id=2}} ).

Reason is, {{boltml run-train}} doesn't know which test you want to run. In {{config.yaml}} you define tests (for now).

So this part is specific to the {{e2e}} command:

{noformat}e2e:
- env: test
  name: dockerized
  run:
  - kwargs:
      local_workspace_suffix: city_id=2
    name: preprocess
  - kwargs:
      local_workspace_suffix: city_id=2
    name: train{noformat}

===

One solution is to define a {{train}} test like this:

{noformat}e2e:
- env: test
  name: dockerized
  ...
- env: test
  name: train
  run:
  - name: train
    kwargs:
      local_workspace_suffix: city_id=2{noformat}

and then run the command:

{noformat}boltml e2e -t train{noformat}

which will run only the {{train}} step with the correct arguments.

===

I'll add also a ticket to enhance {{config.yaml}} so that it supports adding defaults for {{boltml run-*}} commands (so not just {{e2e}}).

===

For now, I'll update the docs with this information as I think is important.

===

Last thing: you can safely commit {{config.yaml}} to the repo. If you do, it won't get regenerated every time. It's main purpose was to replace {{tox -e <test_name>}}  (as we don't use {{tox}} as a test framework, but as a local orchestrator).

Hi [~accountid:62b1c880566f3e7b0a8f2eb7] we don’t have meeting notes. I can briefly summarise what we discussed:

# *Payments:* So far, previous discussions with payment service providers (e.g., City24 or others) around offering suitable payment solutions to make the payment flow happen in a way that Bolt would be fully out of the payment flow have not happened due to legal/tehcnical reasonse (e.g. regarding how the incoming customer payment will be split between Bolt and Liki24 - delivery and agency fees to Bolt; goods value to Liki24). If future technical or legal set up changes occur (e.g., through the City24 project), this may become feasible. However, as there is currently not enough confidence that there is a workable solution ready, legal/FinReg preference would be that we rather aim to find a workable agency/contractual model and use our existing payment flow.
# *Agency model and contractual structure:* Under the current terms with Liki24, Bolt cannot legally act as an agent for either Liki24 or the pharmacies:

* To act as an agent for pharmacies, Bolt would need direct contracts with them, which we do not have.
*  According to the current terms Bolt is assigned as an agent of Liki24. Bolt also cannot act as an agent for Liki24, as Liki24 is not (and cannot be, due to licensing) the seller of goods.
* As a result, Bolt has no legal basis to collect customer payments for goods and forward them to Liki24.

# *Liability:* Liability for issues related to sold goods is problematic. Bolt has no contractual relationship with pharmacies, making it difficult to pursue them for product-related or regulatory claims. Under our current agreement, Liki24 also does not assume liability for such claims, leaving Bolt exposed. 

*PT model under the discussions currently:*

* *Pharmas are independent sellers & have provider profiles:* Each pharmacy signs its own contract with Bolt (onboarding form as an annex to master agreement) and joins Bolt Food individually, but benefits from the commercial terms pre-negotiated between Bolt and Addo Pharm.
* *Payments:* Payments for orders are done directly to pharmas, not to Addo Pharma. So usual flow. 
* *Agency fees:* Bolt pays to Addo Pharma only one time signing bonus.  Pharmas pay agency fees to Bolt as usual. 
* *Addo Pharm supports onboarding and integration*, provides pharmacy data (pricing, stock, location), and ensures pharmacies comply with legal requirements for OTC sales.
* *Bolt applies the agreed commercial terms* to all Associated Pharmacies, provides technical support, and operates the delivery service through its platform.
* *Addo Pharm has onboarding and performance commitments*, including maintaining a minimum number of active pharmacies.
* *Pharmacies remain independent sellers*, responsible for product compliance, preparation, stock accuracy and safety obligations, while Bolt handles delivery and client complaint workflows.

Draft of the initial agreement (WIP): [^AGREEMENT Bolt food Vs ADDO PHARM.pdf]

*_Subject:_* _Clarification on Disability Quota Contribution and Refusals of Fleet Partner Applications_

_Dear Sir/Madam,_
_We refer to recent communication that came to our knowledge indicating that certain applications for the renewal or issue of employment licences / single permits for cab drivers engaged with Bolt fleet partners are being refused or limited to work on other platforms, on the basis that Bolt Support Services MT Ltd (“_*_Bolt MT_*_”) allegedly does not meet labour-market testing requirements linked to the 2% disability employment quota and related contribution._
_We would like to clarify the following points:_

# *_Bolt MT is not the employer of any drivers or fleet partners_*

_Bolt MT does not employ any cab drivers or food couriers in Malta. The drivers in question are employed (or otherwise engaged) directly by independent fleet partners / transport operators, who are the registered employers on the Jobsplus systems and on the relevant employment licences._
_Bolt MT’s employees are limited to corporate support staff (administration, support, etc.), and no drivers’ wages or operating payments flow through Bolt MT._
_It is also important to clarify that the Bolt ride-hailing platform used in Malta is owned and operated by_ *_Bolt Operations_*_, which acts as the digital intermediary between passengers and transport operators. Contracts with passengers and transport operators are entered into with Bolt Operations, and rider fares are settled through payment flows outside Bolt MT’s books._
_In conclusion, Bolt MT does not act as employer or contracting counterparty for drivers or fleets, and is not the entity appearing as “employer” on any of the applications that are currently being rejected or restricted._

*_2. 2% disability quota and contribution – non-receipt of invoice and regularisation_*
_We acknowledge that Bolt MT, as an employer with more than 20 employees, is subject to the 2% quota for the employment of persons with disability and, where the quota is not met, to the obligation to pay the applicable annual contribution._
_However, we wish to emphasise that_ *_Bolt MT never received the contribution invoice_* _at the time it was issued, because it was being_ *_sent by Jobsplus to an old/incorrect address_*_. We only became aware of the outstanding contribution when this matter was raised with us recently.As soon as this was brought to our attention:_

* _We_ *_contacted Jobsplus_*_,_
* _Jobsplus_ *_updated our address in its records_*_, and_
* _The outstanding contribution was_ *_immediately sent for payment on 28.11.2025_*_._

_The delay in payment was therefore due solely to the fact that the invoice was never received at our current address, and_ *_not_* _to any intention on Bolt MT’s part to avoid or disregard its statutory obligations._

*_3. Link to fleet partners’ labour-market testing_*
_Our understanding is that the 2% disability quota and related contribution are assessed_ *_per employer_*_, i.e. by reference to the workforce of the specific legal entity which is the employer of record._
_In the present case:_

* _The employers of the drivers are the fleet partners / transport operators;_
* _Bolt MT is not their employer and does not appear as employer on the Jobsplus employment licence / single-permit applications; and_
* _Bolt MT’s temporary non-compliance with its own quota (which has now been fully regularised) is unrelated to the fleets’ compliance status._

_For this reason, we respectfully submit that it is_ *_not appropriate to treat Bolt MT’s previous quota-contribution issue as a negative factor in the labour-market testing of applications where Bolt MT is not the employer_*_, and to reject or restrict those applications or impose conditions such as “not to work on the Bolt platform” on that basis._

_In light of the above, we kindly request that Jobsplus:_

* _Confirms in writing that employment licence / single-permit applications submitted by our fleet partners, where they are the employer of record and are themselves compliant with their obligations, will_ *_not be refused, restricted or conditioned_* _by reference to Bolt MT’s quota contribution issue, which has now been remedied; and_
* _Clarifies whether there is any specific legal provision or Jobsplus policy that would justify conditioning fleet partners’ licences on drivers_ *_not being allowed to work via the Bolt platform_*_, given that Bolt MT is neither their employer nor the platform holder, and given that the contribution has now been paid following correction of the address issue._

_We remain available to provide any further information you may require, and we are committed to full compliance with Malta’s employment and immigration framework._
_Yours faithfully,_

hey!
I am wondering about the following topic, because of [this|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C062Z0FU5KN/p1764163500350869] discussion.

If we set an {{enrollment limit}} on the test to a specific value (let's say 10M) and this test has campaigns with {{"Max code targets"}} and this value is 5M, there is a significant gap between the enrolled users and the users who will receive this campaign.
Someone who is tracking enrollments and sees 8 million enrollments will be happy and think it's going well, only to be limited by a number from campaigning that is irrelevant to this person.
Why would someone put two different numbers, one may ask?

Well, I understand that we need guardrails to prevent overspending, but currently, most campaign creators ignore the {{max code target}} number, as they want everyone who is enrolled to receive it and enter a large amount just to comply with the required field. In reality, doing so could prevent them from achieving their expected results.

Can we have an option to not input {{max code target}} in a campaign? If it's mandatory, then it could be derived from the enrollment limit if the user does not provide it. wdyt?

[Uladzislau Tolkach|https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/people/6305dd67cf3340e8737f8f66] synced this conversation thread with the Slack thread [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C062940V5JB/p1764254030010519?thread_ts=1764254030.010519&cid=C062940V5JB|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C062940V5JB/p1764254030010519?thread_ts=1764254030.010519&cid=C062940V5JB|smart-link]. Replies in synced threads will automatically update across both Slack and Jira.

Hi! Isn't it possible just to pass the same max_code_target the same as global_enrollment_limit in test?
to derive this value from test it would be tricky, as if you create a campaign without test - there will be no test to derive from.

This is what we currently want to do in automation to prevent errors. But for me, this is a "hack" that does not solve the real issue.

And the real issue is that users don't want this value to limit them, so they set something they believe is large enough so they are not limited.
This means 2 things -
1. If this is supposed to be a safety mechanism, well, it's implemented, but it's not working as intended, so it might be disabled as well.
2. It causes unpredictable situations where this value should have no real meaning when being put in, and suddenly it might become an issue without the creator's realisation.

If you allow users to enter a random, huge number with the intention of ignoring any limits, why not allow this by adding a checkbox {{[x] 'Do not limit code targets}}'?
The result is the same, but what we gain is that we are less prone to errors, and we are not forcing anyone to do hacks.

{quote}users don't want this value to limit them{quote}

I believe that it's actually a safeguard to not to create unlimited campaigns, where even int.max is better than Infinity, and TBH I would explain to users why it's needed. I think it's not only prevents us from uncontrollable money giveaway, but also may be a subject of audits. But I understand the situation and your concerns, let me create a ticket and discuss with the team potential risks.

Under Maltese law and our Passenger T&Cs, the transport contract is between the rider and the Provider (driver/fleet) and any fault-based liability sits with the driver/fleet and their motor insurer, not with Bolt as an intermediary platform.

So in my view we should keep the line that any formal claim needs to be directed against the driver / fleet owner (and their insurer). However, we can of course:
– confirm the trip details;
– give them a contact channel for formal correspondence; and
– if they do send a lawyer’s letter to Bolt, we forward it to the relevant fleet / driver / insurer to handle.

I’d suggest the customer-facing reply below:

_“Hi xxxxxxx,_

_First of all, we’re very sorry to hear about what happened to your wife’s dress and shoes. We’re glad there were no physical injuries, but we fully appreciate this was upsetting and inconvenient for you both._

_Under our Terms and Conditions for Passengers and the local Maltese transport framework, Bolt does not provide the transport service itself. The cab ride is provided by an independent licensed operator/driver, and the contract for the carriage of passengers is between you and that Provider. Any legal claim for damage caused during the ride (including property damage) must therefore be directed against the driver and/or their employer (fleet operator) and handled in line with their motor insurance and the applicable Maltese law._

_If you and your lawyer wish to pursue a civil claim, the correct defendants would normally be the driver and/or the fleet operator (and their insurer). We can help by confirming the identity of the Provider involved and by forwarding any formal correspondence we receive to them._

_If your lawyer still wishes to send a formal letter to Bolt, you can find all relevant information for that purpose_ [_here_|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/legal/tnc-legal-notice/?category=other]_._

_Best Regards,”_

I wanted to clarify that my previous question was not about the general definition of CCPO or FRT and the weekly stats, but rather about the depth and structure of the Delivery dashboards, and how they currently limit our ability to investigate market performance.

*Summary*

The current Delivery CCPO and FRT dashboards do not offer the depth of diagnostic detail required to perform weekly market investigations. Compared to the Rides dashboards, Delivery lacks several critical analytical components that limit our ability to identify root causes, understand persona-level trends, and provide accurate insights to stakeholders.

This request outlines the specific gaps and the required enhancements to bring Delivery reporting in line with existing Rides standards.

*Problem Statement*

The Delivery CCPO and FRT dashboards currently provide only level monthly metrics and limited filtering options. They do not allow week-on-week analysis, persona-level segmentation, or ATI-level movement tracking.

Due to these limitations, TLs and Specialists cannot determine:

* What is driving a CCPO increase or decrease?
* Which ATIs or personas contribute to the trend?
* What specific issues are affecting FRT, TRT, or AHT?
* Where outliers are occurring,
* Or how issue patterns evolve week over week.

This significantly restricts root-cause analysis and delays corrective action.

*Current Gaps Identified*

*1. CCPO Dashboard (Delivery)*

* Only supports *month-on-month* views (no week-on-week).
* Only shows *one month of change* (no multi-period comparison).
* No *ATI-level* CCPO movement.
* No *persona-level* CCPO (Eater, Courier, Provider).
* No view for *Top 10 ATIs* impacting CCPO.
* No *AI vs Manual* comparison in a single view.

*2. FRT Dashboard (Delivery)*

* No combined *FRT + TRT + AHT* persona split.
* No *weekly* FRT or TRT breakdown.
* No *FRT outlier* investigation view.
* No *FRT/TRT/AHT breakdown by issue type* (ATI).
* No visibility into how ATIs impact performance week-on-week.

*Expected Behaviour (Reference: Rides Dashboards)*

The Rides CCPO and FRT dashboards provide:

* Week-on-week metric change tracking
* Persona-level segmentation
* ATI-level performance movement
* Top 10 issues by market
* AI vs Manual contact comparison
* Combined operational KPI views (FRT, TRT, AHT)
* Clear outlier identification
* Multi-period trend analysis

These capabilities enable quick diagnosis, accurate weekly reporting, and actionable insights.

*Requested Enhancements*
*CCPO Dashboard Enhancements (Delivery)*

# Add *week-on-week CCPO* change (not only month-on-month).
# Add *persona split* (Eater, Courier, Provider).
# Add *Top 10 ATIs* affecting CCPO by week.
# Add *ATI-level CCPO changes* week over week.
# Add *AI vs Manual CCPO* comparison in the same dashboard.
# Add *multi-week comparison period (4–12 weeks)*.

*FRT Dashboard Enhancements (Delivery)*

# Add combined *FRT + TRT + AHT* weekly persona split.
# Add *weekly FRT trend* (not only monthly).
# Add *FRT outlier view* (cases with extreme response times).
# Add *FRT/TRT/AHT by issue type (ATI)*.
# Add *week-over-week ATI movement* to identify drivers.
# Add *support case volume + ATI count* in the same table.

*Business Impact*

Without these enhancements, Delivery support teams cannot effectively investigate weekly movements, identify root causes, or provide actionable insights to markets and leadership.

This results in:

* Delayed operational interventions
* Inaccurate or incomplete weekly reporting
* Lack of visibility into persona and issue-level trends
* Increased time spent manually stitching data from multiple dashboards

These improvements will significantly increase reporting accuracy, speed of analysis, and operational decision-making.

Current Findings:

* The current channel logic in the company_data CTE assigns attribution primarily based on promo codes.
* However, for users who do not use promo codes, the attribution defaults are not fully reflective of actual acquisition channels.
* This results in inconsistent channel assignment and partial mismatches with expected marketing attribution.

Solution:

* Updated the company_data CTE transformation to integrate the UTM-based attribution path (ref: [+here+|https://github.com/bolteu/looker-marketing/pull/787/files]).
* Grouped the traffic source values based on discussion with the Business Ads Team. (ref: [+here+|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1jpUP8gXupUXHapNPfYPFP-ZbmexoH42eZ_ncDiQdka0/edit?gid=1450792043#gid=1450792043])

Hi [~accountid:5ccc34a5326cf40e4549d40d]  I’ve pulled the initial numbers to estimate the potential impact of the new rule changes. The figures below are based on 30 days of data using the updated rule conditions + focusing on cases where the checkpoint decision was "pass" (e.g. where we previously did not automatically remove the paid wait fee).

With the new rules in place, we expect to:

* *Remove paid wait fees from an additional ~11.2K orders per month*
* *Prevent ~1.4K distinct refunds monthly*, avoiding approximately 9.6K EUR in total refunded amounts
* *Avoid around 50K EUR in cumulative incorrect paid-wait overcharges per month*

These rules now cover all scenarios from the examples we reviewed and primarily target paid wait fee issues caused by early/late status changes.

I also noticed that many cases from your top reporting countries fall under the “I was charged more than expected” category. This may indicate drivers overcharging beyond paid wait fees. If we can identify some clear overcharge examples, we could explore further refinements to the checkpoint rules to address these cases as well.
However for the paid_wait cases, we now at least have base rules for the trouble markets, so if we get odd reports from these countries regarding the same abuse, it’s much faster to update.

[~accountid:60e96a33131bf80069e145ab] One fairly high level thought: It probably pays to be mindful that (as far as I am aware) there isn’t overly much magic to the special LLM guidance files except being an automatically included *_entrypoint_* (not data source itself).

In reality having one AGENT.md file (or whatever unified structure) and explicitly instructing LLMs to use that has somewhere between 80-100% the same effect. The automated context handling seems to only do two things:
1. Automatically include context. Including structures to help include guidance.
2. *_Maybe_* keep context up to date better, but this seems to be unreliable if such functionality even exists in most LLMs?

Thus it seems like a way forward could be unifying all knowledge into one generic format and simply thinking of a mechanism to just point LLMs towards that source via prompting?

- .cursor/agent.md
- .github/copilot-instructions.md
- .codex/agent.md

We have concluded that the detected infostealer malware *did not exfiltrate data*. Although the malware executed and attempted to communicate with its Command and Control (C2) servers, it did not receive any instructions. Evidence suggests the C2 infrastructure was likely offline or already taken down at the time of infection.

*Remediation Actions Taken:*

* *Containment:* The affected device was isolated from the network upon detection.
* *Credential Rotation:* The user’s Okta password was reset, and existing certificates were revoked.
* *Forensics:* A full investigation was conducted to confirm the scope of activity.
* *Sanitization:* The malware and its persistence mechanisms were removed.
* *Resolution:* The device is now clean, and network containment has been lifted.

[~accountid:5bb1cc64c9dad04734ea835a] Trip’s feedback on our expected push back on clause 5.5

While we understand the conventional stance of platform models to limit direct liability, we believe a more nuanced approach to this clause aligns better with evolving standards of platform accountability and sustainable partnership.

Our comment was intended to address a critical gap in risk management and user trust. A complete exemption of liability, even indirectly, may shield Bolt in the short term but can create significant long-term risks for the ecosystem, including:

Erosion of Trust: The foundation of the platform economy is user confidence. The purpose of a business is to create and serve a customer, which is rooted in trust. A clause that offers no pathway to redress in cases of verified misconduct can undermine this trust for all parties involved.

Reputational Co-risk: Any significant incident involving a driver directly impacts the reputation of both Bolt and its partners. A collaborative framework for investigation and resolution is not just about liability, but about shared responsibility for safeguarding the platform's integrity.

Regulatory Trends: The global regulatory landscape is shifting towards greater platform accountability (evident in directives like the EU's Platform Work Directive). Proactively establishing a cooperative framework positions our partnership ahead of potential compliance requirements.

We are not seeking to assign blanket employer liability to Bolt. Our objective is to ensure there is a defined process for cooperation and a fair mechanism for redress in exceptional [circumstances.|http://circumstances.To]

[To|http://circumstances.To] find common ground, we propose a revised approach to the clause that focuses on these two principles:

Duty to Cooperate: A commitment that Bolt and its sub-fleets will use reasonable efforts to cooperate in the investigation of serious incidents.

Defined Redress Mechanism: Instead of open-ended liability, we could explore a specific, limited solution, such as a process guided by existing insurance policies or a capped passenger guarantee fund for validated claims.

This approach transforms a point of contention into a commitment to safety and partnership. We are confident that we can draft language that acknowledges the nature of your business model while incorporating these essential safeguards.

As a side note - Small Claims Courts in South Africa *do not allow legal representation.* 

Notwithstanding, please see guidance below:

# *Incident Report*
Has an internal incident report been created regarding the alleged fraud? If not, please ensure one is generated so that the matter is properly documented.
# *Driver Account Status*
Please check and confirm the current status of the driver’s account in light of the allegation. 
# *Engagement With the Parties and Privacy Constraints*
## As the matter has escalated to formal legal proceedings, Bolt cannot engage with either party on the substantive issues in dispute. This means CS should *not* contact the driver to ask questions on behalf of the customer or for the purpose of gathering information to support the customer’s case.
## In addition, Bolt is bound by strict privacy and data-protection obligations and cannot share personal data or account information with either party outside the channels permitted by law. Bolt is, however, able to disclose relevant data *when formally required to do so as part of legal proceedings*.
## Accordingly, you should advise the customer that if they require Bolt’s records or cooperation, they should take steps to formally include Bolt to the Small Claims Court proceedings ➡️ {color:#ff5630}*they must request the Commissioner/clerk to issue a subpoena compelling Bolt Operations OÜ to produce documents or to provide evidence.* {color}Once properly cited, Bolt can lawfully provide the information requested.
# *I’ve drafted a suggested response for the client -*
_As the matter is now before the Small Claims Court, Bolt is not permitted to intervene directly in the dispute or communicate with the driver about the merits of the claim. Bolt is also required to comply with strict privacy and data-protection obligations, which means we can only share a driver’s data or account information when legally authorised to do so._
_If you require information from Bolt for purposes of the court proceedings, you may request the Clerk of the Small Claims Court to issue a subpoena addressed to Bolt. Once we receive a valid subpoena, Bolt will be able to disclose the relevant information as required by law. Please let us know if you need any administrative details for service of the subpoena._

More context:

* sorting is done on client-side, here’s how:
** we take all categories that are available *and* contain selected sorting key ({{price_rank}} / {{eta_rank}}) in {{sort_data}}, sort them based on value in sorting key (JFYI: clients parse these values as 64-bit {{double}})
*** tiebreakers are solved via original order from {{/rides/search/getRideOptions}}
** then we append all unavailable categories in original order from {{/rides/search/getRideOptions}}
* that’s exactly what causes this bug and why Bolt Send is in the middle of the list
** there are no {{price_rank}} / {{eta_rank}} because Bolt Send is explicitly disabled in sorting config (see {{CategoriesSortingRepository}})
** setting them to a large value would solve this issue, but I am not sure how viable this solution is – do we add specific category groups to use large hardcoded value in config alongside categories that should be excluded?



Summarizing, there are 2 options:

# Update sorting in clients – add non-busy categories first, and only then add busy
# Update sorting config on BE forcing specific category ids / category groups to pass large hardcoded value for {{price_rank}} and {{eta_rank}} (be mindful about 64-bit {{double}} though)

*_Unfair contract terms_* 

_We have highlighted a couple of terms that we consider may be at risk of being UCTs, depending on how they are applied in practice. For completeness, a UCT is a term that would cause significant imbalance in the parties’ rights and obligations under the contract, is not reasonably necessary to protect the legitimate interests of the party who would be advantaged by it, and would cause detriment to a party if it were applied, enforced, or relied on. Potential at-risk examples (based on the list of examples supplied in the Fair Trading Act itself) are ‘one way’ terms, such as a right for one party to terminate but not the other, or an exclusion of one party’s liability but not the other’s._

_A term is not a UCT until the contract it is in is declared as a ‘standard form contract’ (either a standard form consumer contract or a standard form small trade contract) and the relevant term is declared ‘unfair’ by the court._ 

_Only the Commerce Commission can apply to the court, either on their own initiative or at the request of a party to the contract, for a declaration that a term in a standard form consumer or small trade contract is a UCT. Once a term is declared to be a UCT, it is unlawful to apply, enforce, or rely on it in the affected contract, or to subsequently include it in a new contract, with fines of up to $600,000. There is no liability per se for having included that term in a contract pre-court declaration, but there is a risk that a declaration will then leave terms in the affected contract void which may create some uncertainty as to what the contractual position is on certain matters._

*_Payments service_*

_These terms suggest that the Bolt Balance feature might be a means of payment/value transfer service, with the effect that it could be deemed to be a regulated ‘financial service’ under New Zealand law. The_ [+_Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008_+|https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/___https:/www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2008/0097/latest/dlm1109427.html___.YzJ1OnJhamFoYW5kdGFubjpjOm86OTJhYWZhM2RiYmE1NGI2N2VhNDExZmM3ODQ4ZDljMWQ6Njo5MjQ4Ojc0NWRjZWVkNDRkNzkxMDA0YjJjYzYxODQzMTAxZjMxYzdkOTQ2ODQ4NGJjMTU2NzFlYzU3ODgyODQ2ZjAxNjA6cDpGOk4] _(‘_*_FSP Act_*_’) requires providers ‘operating money or value transfer services’ or ‘issuing or managing the means of payment’ to be registered. How it works
1. An error bottom sheet appears when the getActiveOrder request keeps failing for at least 15 seconds on the price confirmation screen while an information bottom sheet is displayed (e.g., “Waiting for rider to pay”, “Payment method changed”).
2. When the user taps Retry, the bottom sheet is dismissed immediately so it doesn’t block the driver app UI.
3. If getActiveOrder still does not recover, the flow returns to step 1.

How it works: APM flow is based on information messages that comes from `getActiveOrder`
1. error bottom sheet appears when `getActiveOrder` request constantly fails for at least 15 seconds on price confirmation screen and an information bottom sheet is shown, like "Waiting for rider to pay", "Payment method changed"
2. click "retry" immediatly dismisses itselft just not to block driver app UI
4. in case `getActiveOrder` hasn't been recovered, it backs to step 1

How to test:

Note: The error view in the driver app represent only failed network request, not internet connection issues.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

*Internal note*:

The lawyer’s claim that “_the "ride price" column is a data field that exists solely because of the driver's professional activity. It is personal data that drivers must have access to in accordance with the GDPR._” is not a strong argument, and is very unlikely to hold any weight with CNIL/AKI. 

Research:

* +Definition of personal data (Article 4(1) GDPR)+: “‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.”
To decide whether something _relates to_ an individual, you must assess whether it is _about_ that person. In other words, whether its *content, purpose, or effect* concerns them personally.
* +WP29 Opinion 4/2007 on the concept of personal data, pages 9-11+: In general terms, information can be considered to “relate” to an individual when it is _about_ that individual. The Working Party previously noted that "data relates to an individual if it refers to the identity, characteristics or behaviour of an individual or if such information is used to determine or influence the way in which that person is treated or evaluated". In order to consider that the data “relate” to an individual, a "content" element OR a "purpose" element OR a "result" element should be present:
** The “content” element is present in those cases where information is given about a particular person, regardless of any purpose on the side of the data controller or of a third party, or the impact of that information on the data subject. Information "relates" to a person when it is "about " that person, and this has to be assessed in the light of all circumstances surrounding the case.
** The “purpose” element can be considered to exist when the data are used or are likely to be used, taking into account all the circumstances surrounding the precise case, with the purpose to evaluate, treat in a certain way or influence the status or behaviour of an individual.
** The "result" element lies where data can be considered to "relate" to an individual because their use is likely to have an impact on a certain person's rights and interests, taking into account all the circumstances surrounding the precise case. It is not necessary that the potential result be a major impact. It is sufficient if the individual may be treated differently from other persons as a result of the processing of such data.
* +CJEU C-434/16 Nowak+ - also supports this balancing test.
{panel}

Note that this is only the ENG side of the agreement. We will need to accommodate the changes to the bi-lingual version after. 

This is a Cooperation Agreement on Payment Services and Integration between Kapital Bank OJSC and Bolt Services AZ LLC. The purpose is Bolt’s connection to Birpay functionality for users to pay for goods/services via Birbank, with real-time fund transfers after commission deduction. 

+*Some useful terms:*+ 
*Birbank* (section 1.10):

* Software/mobile application provided by *the Bank*(Kapital Bank OJSC)
* Offers payment services
* Includes functionality that enables QR code scanning

*M10* (section 1.11):

* An electronic wallet/mobile application provided by *Pashapay LLC* (a different company)
* Also offers payment services
* Also includes QR code scanning capability

*Birpay* (section 1.9):

* A functionality or product that operates *on both* Birbank and M10 applications
* Specifically enables payments by scanning QR codes
* This is the common payment feature that works across both platforms

Note that *Birbank* and *M10* are two separate mobile payment applications from different providers, while *Birpay* is the QR code payment functionality that works within both of these apps.

+*Duties of the Parties (obligations):*+

* Added an obligation for the bank to notify Bolt for non material changes to the agreement and to ask for Bolt consent for any material change. (4.1.4) 
* Added 15 days period for Bolt to cure any alleged breach. 

+*Settlement:*+ 

Check clause 6 of the agreement. The transfer of the funds collected from each payment shall be done in real time after deducting their commission.  +*Note that the Commission rates table is missing.*+

+*Termination:*+

There are no termination provisions in our favour. I have suggested termination for the bank non compliance with their obligations (regulatory and contractual) and also for convenience with 60 days notice. The original agreement gave the Bank broad unilateral termination rights (4.1.8) with no reciprocal protections for Bolt.

Same with the Liability. I have made suggestions to try to balance an agreement that had no meaningful liability limitations.

By adding Section 5 alongside your termination rights in 4.2.10 and 4.2.11, you've created a *more balanced, bilateral agreement* where:

* Both parties have capped downside risk
* Bolt has exit rights if the Bank underperforms or if its convenient
* The Bank is held accountable for service reliability (particularly important for a payment services agreement where uptime is critical)

We’ve reviewed SICPA’s NDA and made a few targeted changes to align with Bolt’s standard approach and reduce exposure. If SICPA asks, here’s a quick summary of what’s been updated — and why:

# *Termination Clause* – Added a 30-day notice period. This avoids immediate termination, giving Bolt operational stability and time to manage offboarding.
# *Indemnity* – Removed the blanket indemnity for confidentiality breaches. Bolt typically avoids open-ended indemnities in NDAs; standard legal remedies already cover this fairly.
# *Confidential Info Definition* – Narrowed to only include information marked or reasonably understood to be confidential. This limits risk of overreach or capturing routine comms.
# *Remedies* – Softened language around losses and legal costs to avoid disproportionate liability.
# *Governing Law & Jurisdiction* – Updated to England and Wales per our Contract Playbook. This is a well-established neutral framework and avoids complications tied to Swiss law.

After reviewing the facts, my conclusion is *that this does* *_not_* *constitute a personal data breach under the GDPR*.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*Why this is* *_not_* *a data breach under GDPR* 
{panel}

Under Article 4(12) GDPR, a personal data breach requires a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.

Based on the information gathered:

# *No access by individuals outside Bolt or Mixpanel has occurred.*
#* Only Bolt employees with existing Mixpanel access and Mixpanel (as our contracted processor) could view the replays.
#* There is no indication of access by any third parties.
# *Employees who may have had access were already authorised Mixpanel users*, and the exposure happened _within the same controlled environment_.
#* While the masking oversight is a configuration error, it did not result in an access breach by unauthorised recipients under GDPR definitions.
#* Internal over-permissioning cases may still be logged and remediated, but they do not automatically qualify as GDPR reportable incidents.
# *The intrusion risk to data subjects remains very low.*
#* Session replay views cannot be linked to a confirmed viewing of sensitive images.
#* Most replays auto-deleted after 30 days; only ~0.01% of iOS sessions were recorded.
#* Access logs from Mixpanel (70 viewers in last 30 days) do not allow identification of specific sensitive replay views, but this doesn’t change the conclusion, because viewing was still confined to authorised personnel.
# *Mitigation was immediate and effective*
#* New recordings disabled immediately.
#* Mixpanel instructed to delete all stored replays (87k).
#* Risk window has now been closed.

*Internal note*:

* [Consulting|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C09U5U1J0BX] regional legal on whether _droit de communication_ is a valid legal basis for Bolt to share personal data about drivers:

From my research, the _droit de communication_ can be used by French social-security bodies to compel employers or registered entities to produce documents about their *own staff* or *contributors.* Accordingly, the _droit de communication_ creates an obligation only for persons subject to social-security control (employers, insured persons, allocataires, cotisants) and for entities under the administrative authority of the State.

Considering that Bolt’s drivers in France are _self-employed_ rather than employees, and Bolt is not a social-security-affiliated body, French social-security bodies should have no power under these provisions to require information from a digital platform like Bolt about independent contractors. In other words, the _droit de communication_ is likely not a legal basis that can be relied upon when requesting Bolt to disclose data about drivers.

→ Local Ops has been honouring these requests from the RATP concerning drivers. Privacy was not consulted on the validity of the legal basis.

Current possibilities of providing the voucher

* Pre-trigger enrollment: users are enrolled and unique promo codes are generated for all users. The code is provided once the trigger event happens, but not auto applied. Therefore users can see other discounts and compare which one would be better to use (opt-in) as stacking is not possible
* Trigger enrollment: Trigger happens -> the voucher gets auto applied, overriding all existing campaigns or potentially not even being shown due to prioritization logic of vouchers

Adil will look into whether we can do trigger based enrollment without auto applying the voucher.

One major issue that we will have due to current technical set up is the fact that vouchers cannot be stacked. Therefore control group will have BAU incentives while treated group is not BAU + apology voucher, which we would have wanted. An apology voucher should not be a replacement for other vouchers. Thus, if control users receive, on average, the same incentive value from other vouchers (or even more) as our treated group does from apology vouchers, we likely won’t see any uplifts / much smaller ones simply driven by the notification
